https://www.thetimes.com/article/sunak-t.subtitle: The prime minister says people want an end to disruption by ‘noisy minority’
https://www.thetimes.com/article/sunak-t.text:
Rishi Sunak and Suella Braverman are to hold talks with senior sporting leaders and the police in an attempt to head off disruptive protests at Wimbledon and other events over the summer.
The meeting on Wednesday was organised after Just Stop Oil protesters interrupted the second Ashes test at Lord’s by running onto the pitch, hurling orange powder into the air.
One of the protesters, Daniel Knorr, was carried off the pitch by the England wicket keeper Jonny Bairstow after security officials failed to apprehend him.
Targeting sporting events appears to be a change in tactics for Just Stop Oil, which has previously been responsible for traffic chaos by blocking roads during demonstrations against climate change.
Wimbledon, which started yesterday, is on high alert after previous incidents at the Grand National, the World Snooker Championship, and Premiership Rugby final this year.
The All England Club has updated its conditions for entry, with spray paint and glue banned amid fears an environmental activist may attempt to attach themselves to a net. A team of fast runners will also be on duty to beef up security for the third Ashes Test at Headingley this week.
The government meeting, which will also be attended by the culture secretary, Lucy Frazer, is due to discuss how activists can be apprehended before they stage their protests without imposing lengthy security checks on all spectators.
Writing in The Sun, the prime minister praised Bairstow and said government policy would never be set by a “paint-wielding or road-blocking, noisy minority”.
“What I liked most was the matter-of-fact way he did it. He kept calm so the cricket could carry on,” Sunak wrote. “As Bairstow showed at Lord’s, people want an end to this disruption. And I will work with the police and sporting authorities to ensure we do stop it.”
It is hoped the meeting between the prime minister, senior ministers, sporting bodies and police will help deter further protests at sporting events in the coming months.
The Home Office declined to set out which policing leaders and sporting groups are attending the meeting or what countermeasures were being considered.
Sunak said the groups should not command public sympathy because their demands were unreasonable.
“If they got their way life would be truly miserable,” he said. “Extinction Rebellion, for instance, demands we achieve net zero by 2025. That would destroy entire industries, cripple the NHS, throw millions out of work and paralyse the electricity system.
• Just Stop Oil’s protests in pictures: how protesters disrupt daily life
“We will achieve a net-zero economy; but not in a way that kills jobs, and over a period of time, not overnight.”
Sunak said the meeting would “discuss further ways we can reduce the chances of people’s enjoyment being ruined”.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/humza-y.title: Survival has been Humza Yousaf’s only achievement
https://www.thetimes.com/article/humza-y.text:
Nationalist MSPs scuttled off for their long summer break on Friday relieved that they won’t have to deal with any more shocks to the system. There’s been no shortage of those in the three torrid months since Humza Yousaf scraped into Bute House after a chaotic leadership campaign marred by the departure of the party chief executive, Peter Murrell.
Chalices rarely come more poisoned. Yousaf has struggled to lead a party rocked by arrests, resignations, falling opinion polls and other inherited scandals like the delayed Ferguson Marine ferries, the cost of which rose yet again on Friday just as Holyrood went into recess. So what do we make of him so far?
Humza Yousaf was famously supposed to be the “continuity candidate” but he has turned out to be anything but. He’s spent his first 100 days conducting a policy striptease on everything from waste recycling to Nicola Sturgeon’s de facto referendum. What lies beneath? Well, an absence of clothes might seem the obvious answer, pursuing the metaphor to its conclusion. Or is there something more to this than a political leader on the run from unpopular polices? Is Yousaf repositioning the SNP as a centrist party through a conscious uncoupling with its coalition partners, the Scottish Greens?
Sir Keir Starmer has also been discarding policy, ridding himself of the donkey jacket of the Corbyn years. Labour supporters on Twitter are furious at his “lurch to the right” on Brexit, nationalisation, taxation and university tuition fees. The Labour leader has told business to give up its “immigrant dependency”, shelved Gordon Brown’s plan to abolish the House of Lords and delayed Labour’s £28 billion green investment plan. He even called Just Stop Oil protesters “wrong and arrogant”.
What Starmer is doing here is called “detoxifying the brand”. He knows that the left will still vote Labour because there is nowhere else for them to go, so he is trying to appeal to those supposedly socially conservative Red Wall voters who lent their votes to the Tories in 2019. It seems to be working. Labour is consolidating its opinion poll lead over the Conservatives. So is there similar method to Yousaf’s madness? Is he detoxifying the coalition with the Scottish Greens?
The first minister has certainly purged much of the coalition agenda. Yousaf has revised his predecessor’s rhetoric on the North Sea, no longer condemning the development of the Cambo and Rosebank oil and gas fields and even talking about the need for “energy security”. The deposit return scheme, led by the Green co-leader, Lorna Slater, has been returned to sender, as has the Greens’ policy on Highly Protected Marine Areas which almost caused a highland rebellion. It is hard to find anything significant in Sturgeon’s 2021 Bute House agreement with the Greens that still stands. Yousaf has also “paused” the move to ban alcohol advertising. We don’t even have a new national park.
He has of course promised to persevere with the Gender Recognition Reform Bill, currently blocked by the UK government under Section 35 of the Scotland Act. This is supposedly the Green’s red line, the abandonment of which would cause Slater and Patrick Harvie to walk. In April Yousaf ordered his social justice secretary, Shirley-Anne Somerville, to take Westminster’s veto of the Bill to judicial review on the grounds that it is an unlawful restriction on Holyrood’s powers. Some suspect, however, that he is only going through the motions on an unpopular piece of legislation that will most likely get lost in the courts.
Rishi Sunak insists he is not going to introduce the policy of self identification, which allows transgender people to acquire gender recognition certificates by declaration after three months. Scottish gender certificates would therefore not be valid in England, meaning some trans people would change legal sex at the border. This is the kind of constitutional anomaly that the Supreme Court, assuming the issue ends up there, will probably regard as intolerable.
The Supreme Court also rejected Sturgeon’s bill for an “advisory referendum” last year, on the grounds that Holyrood lacks the power to change the constitution. After that rebuff, she called for the next general election to be turned into a “de facto referendum” on independence. If the SNP won a majority of votes, said the SNP constitution spokesman, Mike Russell, Scotland would open negotiations on independence. Yousaf has dropped this idea too, though he has replaced it with a confusing proposal to make “every election” a kind of referendum on independence.
He even suggested that if the SNP wins a majority of seats — not votes — at the next general election he would begin “laying the foundations of an independent state”. No one believes him, even in the SNP. It would be absurd to make a unilateral declaration of independence on the basis of winning 29 seats at the next election. We know and he knows that this is a way of appearing to move the dial on independence without actually doing anything. It is a paper policy, designed to last one news cycle and then be forgotten.
For his part, Yousaf has congratulated himself for making “real progress” in his first 100 days on his real priorities: the NHS, climate change and social inequality. But waiting lists for treatment on killers such as cancer are as long as ever, the climate remains unchanged by his policies and inequality is as wide as ever, even if he has added £15 million to child care for low-income families. Humza’s first 100 days has been all about what he has not done to continue with Sturgeon’s policies, even as he heaped praise on her as the “most impressive politician in Europe”.
But to give him his due Yousaf is, to paraphrase Elton John, still standing. He has negotiated the most difficult three months in the history of the SNP government, defined by the “donorgate” scandal, arrests and that police tent in Sturgeon’s front garden. He doesn’t have any strategic vision, but neither does anyone else in the party right now. This is a government living day to day, crisis to crisis, making it up as it goes along. Perhaps Yousaf, the naked first minister, is the right man for the job.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.title: Archie Manners: how we pranked Just Stop Oil
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.text:
The first thing you notice on entering Just Stop Oil’s “Beyond F***ed Banquet” is the harpist, gently playing relaxing music as the orange-breasted protest group sit down and try to enjoy a plant-based lunch on a sunny Sunday afternoon in Bow, east London. This was a time to relax, to celebrate and to solve climate change with live music and warm white wine.
Tragically, their group had been infiltrated by a producer who works with Josh Pieters and me. We’re professional YouTubers (ask your children) who pull off elaborate stunts. We’re primarily in the entertainment business, but like to try to have a journalistic bent to some of our work. You may know us for having pranked a group of “royal experts” into waxing lyrical on the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s interview with Oprah Winfrey before they had seen it, just to show how all it takes to be a royal pundit is to have shared a taxi once with Princess Margaret and that many don’t always know what they are talking about. Or for having given Katie Hopkins the fictitious “Campaign to Unify the Nation Trophy”.
After weeks of Just Stop Oil’s disruption, we thought it was time to give them a taste of their own medicine. So we attached four 150-decibel personal rape alarms to helium balloons and released them at their banquet. It turns out that the alarms are a lot louder than a harpist, and caused what Just Stop Oil would call “non-violent disruption to prove a point”.
● YouTube pranksters turn the tables on Just Stop Oil
This was the culmination of a few months’ work, but before we discuss just how we infiltrated Just Stop Oil to spark a conversation about their tactics, let me make it clear to the #bekind brigade: obviously, climate change is real and needs urgent solutions.
The problem with Just Stop Oil is simple — those three words are now more associated with slow marching, delayed ambulances and pink hair than they are with climate change. Polls show that the vast majority of the public agree with Just Stop Oil on the importance of tackling climate change, but totally disapprove of their organisation. Their tactics are putting off many people, who look at young Tilly, Billy and Silly and consider killing a polar bear.
Their reputation is that they are an organisation mainly full of privately educated people who can afford to take time off work and spend days standing in the road getting in the way of ordinary working people. Sure, you could say, I am not one to talk; I’m the leather-bound dictionary definition of posh — my Wikipedia page says I am apparently 25th in line to be Duke of Rutland. It takes one to know one, right? But still, I don’t agree with their tactics.
They’ve spent the past 18 months doing what they can to disrupt the public in every conceivable way: from the M25 to Wimbledon and the snooker, the orange people are there, thrilled with their subsequent headlines. They were at Glastonbury, by the way, but they chose not to disrupt that. And as far as anyone can tell, carbon emissions remain unchanged.
Which is why Josh and I decided to infiltrate their organisation — to send in a mole to work out what Just Stop Oil is about, how they work and who they are. This being a complex, high-level membership organisation with carefully orchestrated structures and rigorous vetting, potential members have to go through the rigmarole of providing an email address. Which we did, under the pseudonym of Michael Rawlings. Fifteen minutes later we were added to a series of chats on an encrypted messaging platform called Signal.
These chat groups are where their action is planned, from meeting points for slow marching, to information on who has been arrested and where they’re being held. Non-violence training is advertised, as are film nights and other causes that you might wish to protest for. We were attached to “Group 1”, perhaps because there are only enough active members for a single group, and given our slow-marching orders.
Not wanting to jeopardise our work, we decided to assign one of our producers to the fictional character of Michael Rawlings, who spent the day protesting in Vauxhall as we followed at a distance with cameras. What we learnt was fascinating.
The group met in Pret A Manger. Who can blame them? Pret’s Old Harrovian founder knows how to brew Peruvian coffee. The undercover producer, who is a senior member of the team at our production company Goon Squad, was taking instructions from us through an earpiece and fortunately managed not to go native — a genuine risk given his fondness for beanie hats and people with piercings. He introduced himself as Michael before joining the rest of the group outside, where they gathered. After 20 minutes of casual conversation over rolled-up cigarettes, they started their ritualistic grounding group prayer.
● Just Stop Oil protests in pictures
Our mole secretly recorded footage that showed how Just Stop Oil worked. When one member talks, the others must raise a hand to demonstrate “active listening”, which made them look pretty right wing from where Josh and I were standing. They also don’t applaud, instead choosing to use jazz hands to show support. While it might be better suited to the inside of a Nepalese monastery than the side of London Bridge, the members are clearly kind, well-meaning people, even if their tactics aren’t working.
The police can’t intervene until the protesters have marched on to a road and a Section 12 notice has been served. This system means the protesters spend the day going on to the road, being moved off, returning and being removed again, endlessly, until it’s time for another coffee break. They then return, tailed by the boys and girls in blue, and repeat the same practice before lunch.
It’s then time for the afternoon session, at which some of them decide they’re willing to be arrested. So when the Section 12 notice is issued by the police, they don’t comply with the orders. Instead, they stay in the road, are handcuffed and enjoy a night at His Majesty’s pleasure. The chat groups light up with news that Rupert is being held in Bromley, and others rush to his assistance. Bupa doesn’t offer “arrest insurance”, sadly.
On the second day of our mole’s mission, Josh and I decided to act. So we gathered 15 willing actors, dressed them in “Just Stop Pissing Everyone Off” T-shirts, and used our mole to work out which Pret they were meeting in before surrounding them. By creating a human wall, we prevented them from reaching the road. It made for a powerful picture.
Our mole then discovered they were having their banquet in a church in Bow. We weren’t sure why, given that they claim to “hate” having to protest, but we thought that if they were going to have fun, it should be disrupted too. So we used a prank perhaps better suited to your last day at school, and quite literally raised the alarm. To be fair to Just Stop Oil, their members took it well, and were impressively skilled at bringing the balloons down from the 42ft ceiling. One even tried to improvise a bow-and-arrow to shoot them down, but sadly missed.
Before Josh and I met, my co-conspirator was doing pranks alone, having amassed more than 900,000 followers. I started working for him about five years ago, and during 2020 we joined forces and have somehow built up nearly 1.5 million followers on the platform. As well as creating an awful lot of rubbish, Josh and I have successfully listed a doll’s house on Airbnb and rented it out to unsuspecting tourists to show how easy it is to be conned on the internet; we secretly filmed antivaxer Piers Corbyn accepting £10,000 on the condition that he stop criticising AstraZeneca’s vaccine (it was Monopoly money); and used a lookalike of Ed Sheeran to gain front-row tickets at an international boxing match to show how corrupt celebrity culture is.
I’m a professional magician who still regularly performs, and Josh has a naughty ability to be all things to all people. These are skills that combine to occasionally allow us to bring others with us as we make a point and use laughter to convince people of an argument. It’s all a bit silly, but perhaps there’s a lesson in that for the people of Just Stop Oil. We all know you are right, but as other environmental bigwigs have said, stopping pregnant mothers in traffic and disrupting the cricket is doing nothing for your cause. Either way, more than five million people have now seen our video, so if there’s no such thing as bad publicity maybe you’re the real winners . . .

https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/pare.title: My great big neurodiverse family: six kids, total chaos
https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/pare.text:
I am not sure why my wife, Gemma, a teacher, and I, a stand-up comedian, started having children so quickly and in such high volume. I seem to remember suggesting we should take our relationship to the next level by adding an extra person. Unfortunately she misunderstood my hints and thought this meant starting a family.
Nearly two decades later we have six children, or what I call a Blaker’s half-dozen: Adam, 18, Ollie, 17, Dylan, 15, Zoe, 14, Edward, 13, and Bailey, 9. Three of them have been diagnosed with special educational needs (SEN): Adam and Dylan have autism and ADHD; Zoe, who we adopted when she was two, has Down’s syndrome. Ollie, Edward and Bailey have no official diagnosis, but they do have the surname Blaker, pretty much a diagnosis on its own.
There’s an essay that most parents of a child with SEN will be familiar with called Welcome to Holland by the American writer Emily Perl Kingsley. The central premise is: you were expecting to fly out to Italy for a holiday, and for some reason the plane lands in Holland instead. This was very much us — anticipating one thing and being given another. Although, to be honest, I think Holland sounds too nice for the analogy to truly work.
But you’ll be pleased to know I’m not here to depress you. Quite the opposite in fact. And while there are many things I wish we hadn’t had to go through, looking back I wouldn’t swap our experiences for anything. I love the kids all exactly as they are. Despite what follows.
The problem for me and my wife was that midwives don’t look at parents and say, “Your child is neurodiverse.” In Adam’s case he was diagnosed when he was three; with Dylan it wasn’t until he was six. Therefore even though Adam, our eldest, barely slept for the first year, didn’t feed properly and cried almost nonstop from colic, we decided to have another child a few months later. Adam was still undiagnosed when we concluded that having a two-year-old and a one-year-old (Ollie) wasn’t quite enough work, and started trying for a third (Dylan). I think we’d just decided sleep is for wimps. Had we known the extent of Adam’s needs, then perhaps we’d have quit while we were behind. Instead, in our blissful ignorance, we ploughed on.
Adam’s diagnosis was prompted by his severe speech delay and limited diet. He took eight years to learn to speak, but on becoming a teenager took eight minutes to learn to swear. Were conversations with him bleeped, it would sound like we were living with R2-D2.
Communication has never been Adam’s strong suit. I have a scar on my forehead from the time he threw an Argos catalogue at me and snarled, “You know I like football, so where are my goalposts?” After briefly checking myself for signs of concussion I deduced that Adam had found some pictures of goalposts in the catalogue, and this was his way of saying he’d be grateful if I invested my hard-earned money on buying them. All that plus a side order of reproach for me failing to read his mind and already purchasing them.
It says a lot that, at the time of “Argosgate”, I was so happy that Adam would communicate at all that I was prepared to overlook the fact that this came alongside GBH.
I’m unsure whether it’s due to their needs or merely that they’re Blakers, but my kids don’t do social skills. I hesitate to say they have none at all, but if it’s possible to misjudge a situation, then our children can and will.
Some years ago Dylan asked me whether the bright light in the sky was the moon or a plane. For some reason I replied, “Neither, it’s the Bat-Signal.” I got my comeuppance immediately because his response was, “Seriously?! Batman’s in Edgware?! That’s it, I’m not going to bed until I’ve seen him and got his autograph.”
I’d love to say that he has got better in this area but I’d be lying. Even at 15 he doesn’t really get comedy. Which would be fine, except his father is a professional comedian. Dylan was recently out on a Friday afternoon and texted me to ask what time I’d like him back. Being a world-renowned stand-up/annoying sarky dad, I replied, “6pm. On Monday.” Dylan responded, “But it’s Friday. Why are you saying Monday?” If you really want to know, it’s precisely because of interactions like this one.
The scientists at Oxford University came up with a vaccine for Covid-19 in well under a year, but sadly no one can formulate a food that will be acceptable to all my kids. We’re holding out for taste-free, smell-free and texture-free chicken. If anyone can invent this, give that person a Nobel prize immediately.
Dylan, for example, will only eat food that is white, at a push beige. If there’s a hint of colour — slightly pink, tiny speck of brown or green — that bit must be cut off and destroyed. Pasta may be tubes but never twists. Chips must be long, thin and never crinkle cut. Food should be wholly dry, except when it’s covered in ketchup, which must be evenly spread to his exact specification. Don’t even think about haphazardly shaking a dollop out of the Heinz bottle. It needs to be a thin layer on top of the meal, a meniscus. We can only hope that he isn’t this demanding when it comes to dating, because otherwise he’ll be single his whole life.
Between them the Blaker children seem to cover every variation of SPD, which isn’t a Scottish political party, but stands for sensory processing disorder. They basically have sensory issues. Dylan won’t eat Rice Krispies because he insists they’re too loud. A few years ago he asked me to sift through the bowl and remove the noisiest offenders. I now wonder if he was trolling me or covertly filming for his secret YouTube channel, “Dumb Father Tries to Select Loudest Rice Krispy from Cereal Bowl” — 1.7 million views.
In the 12 years since Zoe moved into our home the question some have asked is, “Do you love Zoe as much as your other children?’ The honest answer, I’m ashamed to say, is no. I love her a lot more. The love one has for an adopted child is so great that it’s possibly among the purest forms of love there is. Obviously I love all my children, most of the time. Yet if we parents are being sincere, there’s a degree of narcissism involved. And the love you have for your spouse isn’t quite as special because in many ways it’s conditional. With Zoe there are no conditions, because due to her special needs she can’t give much back. And that will probably never change.
Like many with Down’s syndrome, alongside her learning difficulties she’s had issues with her heart, mobility, muscle tone, hearing, sight and stomach. The day she arrived my calendar filled up with regular appointments to visit specialists. Meanwhile my car practically learnt how to drive itself to Great Ormond Street Hospital. And crucially, while Adam and Dylan’s autism has become less noticeable as they’ve aged, Zoe has become more demanding. We are now trying to parent a child with the mental age of a four-year-old, but who is also going through puberty and has all the usual hormones starting to race through her body.
Zoe teaches us the inherent value in people. That your worth isn’t defined by what you do or what you achieve. She shows us that people have value simply because they exist. There’s something incredibly special knowing your child was a choice. It’s a privilege to say to your child, “We chose you exactly the way you are and the way you’ll always be because you have worth, and we want to love you.” This child wasn’t the result of one too many glasses of wine (sorry, Adam). They were a choice, and even more so when they have Down’s syndrome. And Zoe was the most rewarding choice we’ve ever made.
Once, while driving down the A5, I was pulled over by the police. “Yes!” screeched Dylan, high-fiving Edward. “Dad’s going to prison! No homework tonight!” Adam had more important issues on his mind: “Dad, if you go to prison, do you think you’ll be someone’s punk or will you be the daddy?”
The policeman approached and spoke to me through my wound-down window, but I couldn’t hear a word for all the chaos in the car, nor could he concentrate on whatever he wanted to say because the kids had now ceased asking me their ridiculous questions and turned their attention to him. “Hey, cop,” Adam said. “Have you got a Taser?” Everyone started squealing in excitement. Then Dylan had a brainwave. “Hey, Adam, get out your phone and film this. We can put it on YouTube and we’ll all be famous!”
“Nice kids you’ve got,” the police officer remarked, kindly ignoring the phone camera now being held inches from his face. It turned out that one of my brake lights had gone, but the officer was so shocked by his encounter with us that it looked like he’d rather have volunteered for a stint with the riot squad. At least Extinction Rebellion protesters don’t also go on and on about Star Wars. Or dinosaurs. Or Marvel movies. The police officer quickly made his way back to his car while I yelled out after him: “Arrest me! I could do with a quiet night in the cells.”
We feel lucky to live in a country with a national health service and state school system that, although underfunded and frustratingly bureaucratic, means we have access to professionals who can give us much of the support we need, all free of charge.
Adam and Dylan are veterans of speech therapy sessions. Knowing the monotonous gibberish they can now come out with, maybe we should have given them a miss. One block focused on teaching conversational phrases, which led Dylan to labour under the impression that “don’t take this personally” operates as a general get-out-of-jail-free card for saying anything that pops into your head. We soon had both a teaching assistant and a mother on the phone complaining about things he’d said along with the caveat “don’t take this personally”. Nor was Gemma too impressed when Dylan said, “Don’t take this personally, but your supper was so disgusting that I couldn’t even get the cat to eat it. Can I have a sandwich?” I was very tempted to call the speech therapist and say, “Don’t take this personally, but why don’t you f*** off?”
Adam attended a mainstream school and was awarded 35 hours of learning support assistant time — the same Zoe now has in her special school. Meanwhile Dylan goes to a regular school with a little additional support.
As you can imagine there have been plenty of phone calls from school, the most remarkable of which is known as “Escortgate”. This involved Adam’s teacher telling us they were concerned about him because during a creative writing lesson he had written that he wanted to hire an escort. I’m puzzled why the school mentioned it, given that:
• Our son was eight.• He had no knowledge of the sex industry. • He was receiving £2-a-week pocket money, which I imagine wouldn’t go very far when it comes to the oldest profession.
Typically the first thing the school did was ask if anything was going on at home, then they called a meeting and showed us his “work”. There was a line that, admittedly, if you squinted at it for long enough could possibly have read “hire an escort”. However, it could just as easily have been “find an escargot”.
No one had thought to ask Adam what he had written. When we finally enquired, he replied, “We had to write words, but I couldn’t think of any words, so I just wrote some letters because letters make up words.” Which is the most brilliantly autistic approach to schoolwork I’ve ever heard. At least we eventually got an apology, and so the story of Adam and the escort did conclude with a happy ending.
Our experiences with Adam and Dylan have convinced me Richard Ashcroft from the Verve was wrong. There was Adam before drugs and Adam after drugs. He was seven when he first started taking Equasym XL. The drugs calmed him down and helped him to concentrate. He was still the same loveable rascal, but it took the volume down from ten to a more palatable six or seven.
Yet, after several years of taking his pills, Adam suddenly became noticeably ruder and more aggressive. We immediately emailed his psychiatrist: “We need more meds now! Up the dose!” This plea was followed by a list of all of Adam’s recent misdemeanours, organised in 73 bullet points, from Argosgate to Jellybeangate (don’t ask). The next day the psychiatrist emailed back: “What you’re describing is normal adolescent behaviour. There is no medication for this. If there were, I would have used it on my own kids.”
As difficult as it can be for parents to find suitable daycare or even a decent babysitter, it all becomes a lot more challenging if it involves a child with extra needs. In Adam’s early years we couldn’t find anyone we felt comfortable leaving him with, so Gemma and I barely had an evening out for the best part of a decade. If you wondered why we kept having children, what else was there to do of an evening?
Even now we struggle more than we might with finding someone to look after Zoe. In truth, nine times out of ten she’d be no problem at all. She comes in from school, turns on her iPad and is happy to entertain herself. But hearing that the job would involve caring for a child with Down’s syndrome is usually sufficient to put candidates off and leave us relying on Adam. Forget the blind leading the blind
Autistic playdates aren’t like the playdates you’re probably familiar with. Those I enjoyed in the 1980s were effectively a day off for both my friends’ parents and my own, as the children scampered off and minded each other, my mum providing some vague supervision from downstairs .
My children are not going to disappear and amuse themselves. Half the time they sit completely apart, playing with separate toys and barely looking at each other. The rest of the time they’re likely to combine their destructive forces like a hurricane tag-teaming with a tsunami. We’ve had drainpipes broken by boys trying to climb up on to the roof; radiators dismantled by boys who wanted to see how they work; and Ikea furniture disassembled by boys who clearly felt they’d outgrown Lego and wanted to move on to something bigger.
Interestingly their friends’ parents have rarely offered to stay. They scarper as soon as possible, dropping their child off with lines like, “Isaac loves it at your house because you’re so relaxed!” Translated this means, “Isaac loves it at your house because it’s even more mental than ours!”
We’re past the stage of loading everyone into the car and taking them out for the day. Now we put it out there and the kids can opt in if they wish. If they want to come, then great; if they’d rather stay at home, lying on their fetid sheets or watching Jurassic World Dominion for the fifteenth time, that’s fine too.
Recently Gemma announced that she would be driving down to the beach. Surprisingly Adam wanted to come, but only on condition Zoe didn’t. On being informed that Zoe was joining, Adam said he’d stay at home, which meant now Ollie changed his mind because his attendance was provisional on whether Adam would be there. Dylan said he’d come if he got to sit in the front and when told he’d be in the back, replied he’d only sit next to Bailey if he was rewarded with three takeaways. Gemma probably thought she’d negotiated well by haggling Dylan down to one, but on seeing this Adam decided he’d come after all, so he could likewise claim a free chicken burger. This brought Ollie back into the picture, but merely until Adam remembered that he’d be working on Monday, so he was out, as was Ollie.
Meanwhile, Edward had initially wanted to stay at home — Jurassic World Dominion won’t watch itself — but, on realising Ollie would be in the house and pulling rank to use the TV, said that he wanted to attend. There are still three days to go, and your guess is as good as mine as to who will end up in the car to the beach.
We’d been told Adam would never get any qualifications, so it’s no exaggeration to say that the day he passed his GCSEs in maths and English was one of the most joyous in our house. He now works at McDonald’s, which he loves, and is thriving. Dylan was selected from more than 1,000 applicants to appear on the BBC series Britain’s Best Young Artist, and we were thrilled.
As challenging as it all is, I’d not have it any other way. We love the kids as they are despite the endless meetings, assessments, therapists, public humiliations, failed playdates, occasional violence, horrific hygiene, and surreal monologues about whether “trees are more intelligent than humans because I saw a video on YouTube that said trees actually had a brain and that if the planet exists long enough then trees may evolve until they can do jobs”.
Gemma and I have needed to truly embrace diversity and accept that our children’s reality is different to ours. They don’t think or act like us and that’s fine. When I order something from Amazon, I don’t lovingly stare at the confirmation email and then track the UPS delivery man like a bona fide stalker. But I know a boy who does, and that’s OK. And in a properly diverse world all approaches are fair and should be respected.
We all have visions of what our children will look like. Usually this involves them being miniaturised clones, combining our best qualities and interests. But this is illusory. The real task of parenting is to make peace with what you’ve been given; to offer unconditional love and support without trying to turn them into something they’re not; and then to celebrate them and enjoy it all as much as you can.

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/art/art.title: Grayson Perry: ‘There’s a delusion that good politics is good art’
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/art/art.text:
It isn’t polite to stare at a gentleman’s legs, no more than it is a lady’s, but I’m staring at the pattern on Grayson Perry’s dungarees. Are those dozens of little what-I-think-they-ares? When I get home I very gingerly put “vulva dungarees” into Google. They are by Lucy & Yak in collaboration with the designer Sanna Suvi and intended to “normalise the conversation and stigma around vulvas, vaginas and periods”. They have sold out online.
It was agreed in advance that Perry wouldn’t be in full rig for the interview or photographs. No costumes, no crinolines, no alter ego Claire. Just his civvies: dungarees, yellow T-shirt, pink Crocs and a heart-shaped badge made of broken enamel. His nails are oval, long and red. How does he clean out the clay?
As for the conversation, it is . . . normal. Chatty, relaxed, easy and punctuated by Perry’s piratical, Strepsil cackle. In the interview transcript I’ve got it variously as: “A-ha. A-ha. A-ha”, “Har. Har. Har” and “Hach hach hach”. He likes a giggle, does our Grayson.
I say our Grayson because this former young Turk, this working-class Essex lad, this tabloid-baiting “transvestite potter” who won the Turner prize in 2003, is one souvenir tea towel away from becoming a full-on national treasure.
I meet the newly ennobled Sir Grayson in his studio in Islington, north London, two days after he was knighted at Windsor Castle by the Prince of Wales for services to the arts. I tell him I don’t know whether to bow or curtsy. “Hargh. Hargh. Hargh.” The honour was accepted on Perry’s behalf by Claire in burgundy puffs. The outfit inspiration was Stuart. “I thought it would just be funny to kind of start off with the last time we had a Charles on the throne. So I looked at those 17th-century portraits, you know, the women with their voluminous taffetas.”
The sort of portrait you would find in the revamped National Portrait Gallery, where Perry was photographed in interstellar chiffon at the opening bash the week before. A few days after our interview, I arrive at the Spectator summer party to find Perry and his wife, Philippa, a psychotherapist and bestselling author, locking their bikes up. Later, I spot Perry, in a neon pink, pie-crust collared babydoll dress, deep in conversation with the foreign secretary, James Cleverly. A few nights after that, Perry is at the South Bank Sky Arts Awards in shiny lamé and with a bow in his unbrushed hair. He designed this year’s award: a riff on a traditional Staffordshire figure that replaces the usual ceramic King Charles spaniel with a cat (Perry’s a cat person) with the face of Melvyn Bragg. There is a litter of Bragg cats, fired and ready, on top of the kiln when I visit. At the ceremony, Salman Rushdie takes home the cat for outstanding achievement.
A knighthood. Doing the summer season. A reference to weekends at “our place in the country”. What class does Perry identify as now? “A-har-har-har. Well, I’m someone from a working-class background who’s firmly part of the elite now.” The liberal, metropolitan, Islington elite? “Yep. Definitely. That’s the nature of the class-elevator that is culture.” Culture — that’s what we’re here to talk about. The dresses? The pussybow blouses? The dirndls, appliqué and quilted bed jackets? Don’t let them distract you. Perry is serious. He is, after Bragg, our best broadcaster on the arts. An hour talking to Perry is like an encounter with Kenneth “Civilisation” Clark putting the world to rights in the Dog and Duck.
Years ago I interviewed Antony Gormley. It was good of him to make time for a student journalist, but he responded to my first question with: “Of course you know what Heidegger said?” I didn’t then and I don’t now. Perry doesn’t talk Heidegger. The closest he gets to an academic citation is mentioning Harry Hill. But in his pots, his tapestries, his documentaries, his books, his teases on Staffordshire-ware, portrait miniatures or wayside shrines, he asks us to think about art, craft, creativity, taste, class and our country, right or wrong, Leave or Remain.
● Sir Grayson Perry’s smash Scottish show is all it’s cracked up to be
I’m talking to Perry before his big Edinburgh retrospective, which runs to November. This week, he posted a photograph on Instagram (his account is @alanmeasles, named after the childhood teddy bear that has been his lifelong companion, muse and sparring partner) of a tartan shortbread tin in the giftshop. It carries a photograph of Perry, taken for the Country Life girls-in-pearls slot, done up like Queen Elizabeth in a silk headscarf, Barbour and sensible skirt. He doesn’t go for my suggestion that he should have an official coat of arms drawn up by the heralds.
The show is called Smash Hits. A potter’s joke. Perry is serious, but funny with it. “I’m fascinated by this tension around seriousness because, you know, increasingly, if I’m an activist about anything, it’s about humour. And the art world seems to think the opposite of serious is humorous. But that’s not true. The opposite of seriousness is triviality. Humour is not a trivial thing. It’s a hugely profound part of being human. And I think it’s a red flag when part of the culture can’t laugh at itself.”
We talk about “international art English”, the theoretical, polysyllabic, post-sense dribble that makes its way onto gallery captions and curatorial blurbs. I put it to Perry that what people like about him is that he doesn’t talk down, he doesn’t dumb down, he just talks like a normal, interested, intelligent person. “They’re scared,” he says. “Scared. I think they’re scared that somehow the audience will see the bottom of their void.” Do they realise that their jargon scares off and puts off audiences? “Yeah, I think they do. It’s a very defensive thing.” He talks of a “status race”, of ever greater “pomposity” and incomprehensibility. How do you set yourself apart, make yourself superior? You talk above the heads of those you wish to exclude.
In his Smash Hits catalogue essay, he talks of moving to London and feeling “a bit of a hick”. Has this hickish feeling left him? At first, he says, “I was intimidated by the trendiness of the people that I encountered. And, you know, I got used to being with them. And then I realised that my hickishness was actually an advantage because it kept me slightly out. I didn’t buy into trendiness. I think one of the threads through my entire career and my attitude to the art world is that I’ve never bought into the idea of avant-gardeness, or the politics of the art world, or the belief in the current trend.”
And what is the trend today? “The -ism of now is activism.” So Extinction Rebellion? Endlessly talking about climate change? “Yes, this sort of delusion that good politics is good art. I want to go, ‘Yeah, I think it’s great. But don’t put it on the wall.’ ” Perry has a Venn diagram he likes to show to students. In one circle: “Things you care about.” In another: “Things you like the look of.” In the third: “Things that hipsters haven’t noticed yet.” In the intersection of the three: “Your art.”
At the moment, he says, “there’s a big emphasis with activists about what you care about. But they haven’t looked at many things. And, you know, I just think that I’m looking for the exquisite.” One of the most moving sections in Perry’s memoir Portrait of the Artist as a Young Girl, written with his friend Wendy Jones, describes visiting the “treasure trove” of the ceramics galleries at the V&A and discovering the slipware dishes of Thomas Toft. “There was a certain old-worldly, half-timbered pubness about his work that I liked.” It’s a moment of artistic awakening, of looking outside oneself and finding a means of expressing what’s within.
Perry might once have been a hick, but he is also, at heart, a hack. He wrote an arts column for The Times between 2005 and 2007. Does he still read The Times? I spot a cutting on his workbench when I follow him next door as he adds another layer of glaze to a tile. “Yeah. I stopped reading The Guardian. The Guardian has changed. It’s lost its sense of humour. I dunno, it just became po-faced.”
Perry still knows how to give good copy; provoke; stir the slipware pot. Now that he is no longer a trustee of the British Museum, what would he do with the Elgin Marbles? “Ha ha ha ha ha ha. Well, that’s down to my personal taste. I’ve never been fond of white statuary, anyway. When I did my show there, Ian Jenkins, God bless him, he’s dead now, but he was such a lovely character, he was head of Greek and Roman. He really took me under his wing, tried to get me liking white statues, though of course they were painted originally. But I used to say, ‘I’ve got such an allergy to clichés. I can’t look at them.’ ”
When we get onto identity politics he becomes half passionate, half sad. I review a lot of exhibitions where we are told that the artist “identifies as queer” or non-binary, or trans, and that their work “explores ideas about queer identities”. The sum of who they are and no more. “That’s what my whole show is about. It’s that,” Perry says. In September, he will tour the country with his one-man gig A Show All About You. “There’s this weird narrowing idea about who people are. I want to look them in the eye and say, ‘Is this really the most interesting thing about you?’ ”
What does Perry make of the battle of the captions being waged in galleries? “Well, museums have fallen into the activist moment as well, haven’t they? All museums now are relabelling themselves in a mad catch-up with the progressive agenda. There’s a justifiable rebalancing in these things. But you know, it’s also very prone to parody.”
Captions all too rarely talk about how art is made. In the Smash Hits catalogue there are illuminating chapters on “pottery technique”, “print technique” and “tapestry technique”. “One of my beefs about the liberal elite,” Perry says, “is that they’re, you know, in their over-educated bubble. They’re dead from the neck down. They don’t have bodies or emotions, they just have thoughts and ideas. And I think that art has been dragged that way a bit. And so, in keeping an emphasis on craft, it’s your body in heavy negotiation with material and your eye reacting to surfaces and textures. And that old-fashioned build-up of sensitivity to that is the centre of art. You know, like just being able to put two colours next to each other, and then for it not to make you sick. That’s really one of my bugbears: how you can be an artist and have bad colour sense.”
Perry is in retrospective mode before Edinburgh. How would he like to be remembered? “I think I’d be a sort of ‘cult artist’. Teenagers would find me and go, ‘He’s mine.’” He mentions being a huge Aubrey Beardsley fan when he got into art. “I think I’m going to be one of those niche people.”
Niche, but establishment too. Now that he’s got an “in” with the royals, is he the man to take on the fourth plinth in Trafalgar Square? Surely it’s got to be an equestrian monument to Elizabeth II, bronze Barbour and all? “Yeah,” he muses. “I dunno if I’m the person, though. Where do you go with it? Weirdly, I’m working on an equestrian thing for another show I’ve got. But in terms of that sort of stultifying realism . . .” He trails off.
“Monument sculpture around London,” he says, lowering his voice to a whisper. “God, there are some dreadful ones.” Is he prepared to name and shame? “I’m fed up with anything that’s minimalist and stainless steel. That whole tasteful, bland thing. I’d rather have the super-realist bronze than a piece of minimalist, symbolic stainless steel that looks like an award you’d get from the Lawnmower of the Year Society.”
Perry can’t be doing with bland or tasteful. “We sneer at people who give in to sensual delight. To pull back from urges is somehow classy. And that goes right through history. You see it time and again. You see it with minimalism. You see it with pared-back, decoloured interiors. Those grey, beige houses — I want to smash them.”
Go to Perry’s show in search of sensual delight and the exquisite. Just don’t get too carried away by aesthetics. No lemon-sucking art appreciation allowed. Look for the jokes. And when you get them, in the hush of those hallowed museum halls, give a good, loud Grayson Perry belly laugh. He-he, ha-hah.
Grayson Perry: Smash Hits is at the Royal Scottish Academy, Edinburgh, to November 12 (nationalgalleries.org)

https://www.thetimes.com/sport/formula-o.title: Lewis Hamilton keeping Brad Pitt on track on Silverstone film set
https://www.thetimes.com/sport/formula-o.text:
As if Formula One wasn’t glamorous enough, Silverstone will have a sprinkling of A-list Hollywood stardust this weekend as the Northamptonshire circuit doubles up as a film set while also hosting the British Grand Prix.
The film, which has the working title Apex, stars Brad Pitt and is directed by Joseph Kosinski. Its makers have been granted special access to the Silverstone paddock and pits where they have even set up a garage for their fictional APXGP team. Their race car, a modified Formula Two machine, will also run a few laps to gather on-track footage.
In much the same way as the 1966 classic Grand Prix, the new film will mix real-life racing footage and cameo appearances by present drivers with fictional scenes involving actors.
Pitt plays the part of an ageing driver who is desperate to recapture former glories. In that regard it would be cruel to suggest that Lewis Hamilton is the perfect man to serve as an adviser and production partner, not least because the seven-times former world champion, who has not won a race since December 2021, is so keen to be involved.
Hamilton, 38, has already done a lot of background work on the film and was clearly happy to see that things are now moving at ground level.
“It was really exciting to see Jerry [Bruckheiner, the film’s producer] walking in,” Hamilton said. “I haven’t been to see the garage yet, but I was here a few weeks ago watching Brad practise. It is massively exciting to see it all come together and finally start filming this weekend.
“There are nerves, naturally, because it’s something we’ve been working on for so long. We want everyone to love it and really feel that we encapsulate what the essence of the sport is all about. That’s our goal and we hope we can do it proud.”
At 59, Pitt is perhaps a little old to be making his grand prix debut — the oldest driver to compete in F1 was Louis Chiron at the 1955 Monaco race — but Hamilton said he had been impressed by the actor’s fitness levels and racing instincts.
“Brad looks like he’s ageing backwards,” Hamilton said. “Of course that was a big topic at the beginning when we were discussing the first story. But he’s super-fit and he’s been training hard.”
While racing traditionalists may feel uneasy about the film crew’s presence at an actual race, Hamilton insisted that the end result would give the sport a huge boost.
“I don’t know if this would have been possible ten years ago when the old management was in place. They wouldn’t have perhaps seen this as an important step in terms of the sport’s growth. But we’ve already seen the great work and impact of the Netflix show [Drive to Survive] and I think this will take it to new heights beyond that.”
Hamilton also reiterated his support for the cause espoused by Just Stop Oil activists, but said he hoped there would be no repeat of the incident at last year’s British Grand Prix when a number of them broke through security and sat down on the track.
“From my perspective and my team’s, we are very focused on sustainability,” he said. “We believe in what people are fighting for and we are making changes as a sport. But safety is key.
“We don’t want to be put in harm’s way and we don’t want anyone else to be in harm’s way. If there was to be [a protest] we hope that it is not on the track.”

https://www.thetimes.com/article/inside-.title: Inside George Osborne’s wedding: the EU anthem rang out
https://www.thetimes.com/article/inside-.text:
In the once-sleepy Somerset town of Bruton, the great, the good and the neither of the British establishment gathered for the wedding of one of the area’s most notorious residents.
At Castle Cary station — a short hop from London — I run into a lost-looking Ed Balls: tanned, casually yet expensively dressed and struggling to find a taxi. He is here for the wedding of the man with whom he will soon launch a podcast — George Osborne, the former chancellor.
Osborne, 52, who not long ago bought a £1.6 million house in the town that has become known as the Notting Hill of the West Country, was marrying Thea Rogers, 40, his chief of staff from the Treasury days.
Hanging over the proceedings was a vicious anonymous email, which makes claims about the couple’s private lives and was sent to guests last week. Osborne has asked the police to investigate, describing the missive as “part of a very serious campaign of ongoing harassment”. The couple are said to know the identity of the person behind the email.
This weekend in Bruton was even better than most for celeb spotters. Over breakfast in At the Chapel, a Daylesfordesque hotel in the town centre where some of the guests are staying, I was briefly excited that I had spotted Samantha Cameron. I hadn’t. A lot of people here look like Samantha Cameron.
I spotted Michael Gove, tie off, lighting up a cigarette in a picturesque alleyway off the high street. Later, he’s pictured walking into the wedding with an iPad under his arm.
But it is outside St Mary’s Church — a beautiful 14th-century building in the town centre — at 4pm that the big guns start to arrive. David Cameron, the former prime minister, looking tanned, with his wife Samantha (actually this time); William Hague , the former Tory party leader and Osborne’s former boss; — Sajid Javid, the former chancellor; Matt Hancock, the former health secretary; and Mark Carney, the former Bank of England governor.
Then there’s Nick Robinson, the former BBC political editor and Rogers’s former boss, and Jon Sopel and Emily Maitlis, former BBC employees but now with Global.
The town feels rather like what you’d get if you asked someone who had never left Notting Hill to draw what they think the countryside looks like: all Farrow and Ball and artfully distressed wooden floors.
Many of the fashionable set are now eschewing the Cotswolds in favour of this little slice of West London in the West Country: the film director Sam Taylor-Johnson and the fashion designer Stella McCartney have also made Bruton their home.
‘The locals don’t like the posh people moving in and putting up the house prices,” Graham, 88, who arrived here a few years ago, tells me. He — along with several others — has turned up outside the church, as he puts it, out of “nosiness”.
Jane, 60, who was born in Bruton, says the same. ‘The whole Notting Hill set thing is ripping the heart out of the town,” she sighs. Why is she here at the church? She grins. “I’ve read the email.”
Rogers, a former BBC producer, became Osborne’s chief of staff in 2015. Her arrival heralded a change in the man. Before her appointment, Osborne “looked like the pasty chancellor who never left the office”, one colleague from the time recalled.
Osborne took up the 5/2 diet on Rogers’s instruction. He got a new haircut, spruced up his wardrobe. But the same colleague was keen to point out that this was not the extent of it: “She had a big impact on altering his public perception.” Even those who don’t like her agree she is a sharp political operator.
The exact nature of the chancellor’s relationship with his most senior aide was a matter of fascination in SW1 for years. “They have always been an enigma,” one former colleague recalls. “Whether or not they were a couple has always been a long-running conversation in Westminster.”
Several former colleagues told me this week that there were always hints — some subtle, some seemingly less so — that their relationship was more than professional. But was it?
“Everyone thought it, but it was never confirmed,” a contemporary said.
Then, finally, in 2020 Osborne appeared on the front page of The Times, resplendent in blue dad-jeans and New Balance trainers. “I have a girlfriend. I’ve never been happier”, read the headline. His 2019 divorce from his wife of 21 years, Frances Howell, 54, was “amicable”, he said.
The former chancellor, it is fair to say, has done well for himself since leaving No 11, developing a penchant for expensive cars. His vast array of jobs has been a cause for amusement in SW1: editor of the Evening Standard, adviser to the asset manager BlackRock (£650,000 per annum), visiting fellow in the United States (“Professor Osborne” to his students). Oh, and he also joined his brother’s firm 9Yards, another venture capital firm.
In April 2021 he jacked it all in to join Robey Warshaw, the boutique Mayfair-based City advisory firm. Safe to say it doesn’t pay badly. Last year Osborne received a share of a £26.5 million payout to four senior staff at the firm. He is also chairman of the British Museum.
Rogers, meanwhile, has kept a lower profile since leaving government. For five years she worked at the food delivery firm Deliveroo, rising to the role of chief customer officer. She was famous among colleagues for her exacting standards, and for the fact that Osborne — with whom she was not then publicly linked — would turn up randomly at the office.
Last year, however, Rogers made the decision to step down. “My maternity leave has given me the chance to reflect on what I want to do next,” she said.
“And now is a great time for me to begin a new chapter as well as to spend more time in the next few months with my baby, Beau.” Beau was joined by a second son, Arthur, last December. Osborne has four children in total.
There is a sense perhaps that the Osbornes are now looking for a quieter life. But as the bride arrived in a classic blue Mercedes, accompanied by her father and several friends carrying umbrellas to shield her from the rain, half of Bruton, numerous photographers and a man dancing around dressed as a teddy bear turned up to enjoy the show.
Afterwards, the couple left through a tunnel of wellwishers throwing confetti — and a Just Stop Oil protester adding her own orange version — with Osborne carrying their older child. David Cameron filmed the scene on his phone. Heading to the reception, at the luxury art gallery event space Hauser & Wirth, guests told me the couple left the church to Be My Baby. After they said “I do”, Ode to Joy — the EU anthem — was played.
You can’t help but feel the quiet life the happy couple crave is some way off.
