https://www.thetimes.com/article/irish-k.title: Irish know a thing or two about a send-off
https://www.thetimes.com/article/irish-k.text:
My sample may not be large enough to be representative — two versus around 15 — but in my experience Irish funerals are better than English ones. Most of the English funerals I’ve been to have taken place in buildings reminiscent of continental railway stations from the fascist period. Perhaps crematoriums are designed that way to convey a sense of human powerlessness in the face of death, perhaps it is to signal a transit point into the next life, or maybe the architects just weren’t trying. The service is punctual and brief, an officiant says some generic stuff about somebody they didn’t know, the coffin shuttles into a furnace and the congregation is hurried out. As it emerges, the next shift is waiting to go in.
The Irish funeral I went to at the weekend took most of two days. On the morning of day one, the undertaker delivered the body back to his home in an open casket. Chairs were laid out for people to sit, chat and think about their friend, who lay looking very much himself, with his old red scarf around his neck. “He’s been so nicely done up,” everybody said. In the next room was tea, wine and whiskey, along with sandwiches, sausage rolls and the cherry cake served in the house since the beginning of time.
Talk was of the difficulty of keeping the sheep off the lawn, the return of salmon to the river and the corpse’s full and varied life. “He left nothing on the pitch,” said one chap, who explained it was what sports commentators said when a player had given his all.
On the morning of day two, there were poems and a eulogy on the lawn beside the river. The rain, which had been pelting down all week, held off for a blessed hour, and the sheep kept a discreet distance. Then the hearse and the mourners processed through the little town, whose inhabitants lined the main street, to a church where a Protestant vicar and a Catholic priest shared the prayers. My friend had no enthusiasm for religion, but plenty for Ireland’s success in replacing communal violence with harmony.
Perhaps the Irish are better at death than the English, or Catholics than Protestants, or small towns than cities. Whichever, it was a good way to go.
People tend to behave worse in crowds than they do singly, but Wimbledon is a powerful counter-example. Last week I watched the Spanish No 1 seed, the astonishing Carlos Alcaraz, beat an unfortunate Frenchman, Jeremy Chardy, to a pulp. The crowd was awed by Alcaraz but kind to Chardy, clapping wildly when he got a point and roaring long and loudly when, well into the second set, he won his first game. The imbalance meant that it wasn’t a great match, but for me the crowd redeemed it. We do, sometimes, have exquisite manners.
At a party recently, I found myself explaining to an elderly acquaintance that one of the younger guests was trans.
“So he used to be Jamie and now he’s Jane?” she asked.
Nearly but not quite, I answered: he was now they.
“Oh dear,” she said. “It’s all so muddling.”
That seemed to me to sum up perfectly the feelings of many older people towards everything trans. There’s the fear that unfamiliar notions normally arouse, and there’s the worry of getting something wrong: it isn’t hostility, but younger people often read it as such.
On Saturday a protester disrupted George Osborne’s wedding by throwing orange confetti on the couple as they left the church. If anyone thinks this wheeze (applauded by Just Stop Oil, though it denied responsibility) is a good tactic, they’re wrong. The British do not like intrusion into personal lives. It’s a breach of manners that goes against the national grain (see above) and will harm protesters causes.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/electri.title: Electric planes: how near are we to take-off and what are the obstacles?
https://www.thetimes.com/article/electri.text:
Dale Vince is confident he will be able to take you on a zero-emission plane in just three years’ time because he has already made synthetic diamonds out of carbon removed from the air.
“Making diamonds from atmospheric carbon, that’s a proper challenge, right? That’s a frontier breakthrough in science and technology,” said Vince, who founded the green energy firm Ecotricity and is thought to be worth about £107 million. “Getting a licence from the Civil Aviation Authority is something that’s been done before. It’s a well-trodden path.”
Yet making carbon-negative jewels could be the easy bit, compared with using relatively new technology to “green up” an industry with rigorous safety standards and a duopoly of large planemakers.
Vince said this week that his new Ecojet airline would carry people on hydrogen-electric planes that produce nothing more than water by 2026.
A donor to Labour, the Green Party and Just Stop Oil, he built a successful small company in Ecotricity but also has a record of big promises that don’t always pan out. In 2016 he pledged five “mills” turning grass into “green gas”, but only one should be operational by next month.
Nonetheless, the entrepreneur has put £1 million of his own money into start-up costs and is looking to raise £10 million for the new venture.
He is far from alone in seeing hydrogen as a key way to decarbonise an industry that accounts for at least 2.5 per cent of global CO2 emissions. Pioneers across the world have said that turning hydrogen planes into a commercial reality will be a big challenge, but also a huge environmental and economic opportunity.
Hydrogen appeals to plane manufacturers and airlines because it’s light compared with batteries, can be stored as a gas or liquid, and governments are supporting ways of producing it in a low-carbon fashion.
“Hydrogen is an important part of the mix because it will yield an aircraft which is producing water,” said Andy Reynolds, head of hydrogen storage and distribution systems at Airbus. “So we escape from CO2 — and potentially, depending on the technology we choose, any of the environmental impacts of aviation, such as contrails.”
Industry players such as Airbus are eyeing 2035 for an A320-sized commercial hydrogen flight. But the first hydrogen plane that passengers are likely to fly in will be much smaller and built outside of the Airbus Boeing duopoly.
Like Airbus, some of those smaller firms are using entirely new plane designs. However, most are retrofitting existing kerosene-powered aircraft because it’s quicker and cheaper. Ecojet is looking to convert a 19-seat DHC-6 Twin Otter and 70-seat Dash 8, with the aim of flights in 2025 and 2027 respectively.
ZeroAvia, which is based at Cotswold Airport in Gloucestershire, has just completed its first round of test flights for a 19-seat Dornier 228, which became the largest hydrogen-powered plane to take to the air in January. Its record was quickly eclipsed by Universal Hydrogen’s test flight of a 40-seat ATR 72 in March.
“Economically and environmentally, this is a superior solution, said James McMicking, chief strategy officer at ZeroAvia. “The one challenge it has, which obviously we’re working hard on, is how quickly can we scale the technology. We know we can power a 19-seat aircraft. We’re working on the technology required to power 80-seat.”
Most smaller plane makers are pursuing one of two ways of using hydrogen. ZeroAvia, Universal Hydrogen and Australia’s Stralis are all piping hydrogen into a fuel cell inside the plane which converts it into electricity. That powers an electric motor that drives a propeller. The alternative is burning the hydrogen, much like kerosene, to power a jet engine. Airbus is exploring both routes.
Bob Criner, co-founder of Stralis Aircraft, thinks fuel cells will win because of lower maintenance costs and the fact there is no risk of contributing to climate change.
“Hydrogen electric systems have less moving parts and operate at much lower temperatures than combustion engines and therefore have significantly reduced maintenance costs,” he said. “Combusting hydrogen eliminates CO2 emissions — however, it still produces other harmful emissions such as NOx, sulphates, particulates and soot.”
The smallest planes can use hydrogen in its gaseous form, but for the 70 to 80-seat scale, McMicking says liquid hydrogen is needed to get the required volumes of fuel on board without a heavy storage tank.
As well as balancing weight and space for fuel cells, tanks and other kit, technical challenges largely revolve around safely generating so much electricity and moving it around the plane. There are various hurdles around heating and cooling. Water or air is needed to keep fuel cells cool. Those wanting to burn hydrogen have to “condition” it up to an acceptable temperature for engines, from what Airbus calls a “bone-numbing” -253C when it’s a liquid.
Other engineering headaches are mundane. “It sounds crazy, but just finding a pipe that can carry liquid hydrogen at -250C, all the way from the tank to the engine without enough heat getting in there to boil, that’s a challenge,” Reynolds said.
Setting aside hurdles in the air, there are many challenges on the ground. A Royal Society report said that producing all the hydrogen needed to replace UK jet fuel would require more than three times the UK’s entire renewable electricity capacity in 2020. It will also need 34 million tonnes of water a year, which electrolysers split into hydrogen and oxygen. Airports will also need hydrogen fuelling infrastructure, which no big UK airport has yet.
Hydrogen fuel will initially cost more than kerosene, but Jayant Mukhopadhaya, of the International Council on Clean Transportation, an American organisation, points out that the biofuels that airlines are exploring today to cut emissions from conventional planes are more expensive than kerosene too.
The top concern for many is how quickly regulators, such as the Civil Aviation Authority, allow hydrogen planes to take off. “Number one is going to be around the certification process for bringing these new technologies to market because it’s very novel,” said McMicking, who is already working with the CAA’s consulting arm to pave the way.
If hydrogen planes do clear regulatory hurdles, there is no guarantee they will reduce aviation’s overall carbon footprint. Initially they might just increase flight numbers rather than replace existing ones.
The small size of the first planes means they might displace some kerosene-powered flights, such as to the Highlands and the Isles of Scilly.
But McMicking sees “new connections being made between poorly served regions”, with hydrogen planes connecting up smaller, underused airfields.
“If you take a family and they want to fly to the Lake District from the south, they will do it with less environmental impact on one of our planes than is in a diesel or gasoline car,” he said. Ironically, Vince said Ecojet’s first route might be one popular with oil workers, Aberdeen to Southampton.
To make a significant dent in emissions, Reynolds wants a hydrogen plane similar to the A320’s typical capacity of 140-170 passengers. With today’s technology he “can’t quite see” how fuel cells get to that scale.
He says hydrogen fuel cell planes could be “a bit less noisy” for passengers than jet engines burning fossil fuels. But as an engineer he mostly wants the planes to be “completely normal” for travellers.
Mukhopadhaya said: “Hydrogen combustion aircraft will likely be bigger than conventional aircraft for the same passenger capacity. But otherwise, I don’t think the passenger experience will be any different.”
He thinks 2026 is an “aggressive” timeline and that the first commercial hydrogen flights will take off in 2027.
Vince, like several of the hydrogen plane makers, claims lower maintenance costs will offset higher hydrogen prices enough for tickets to be the same cost as on polluting planes.
“That’s wonderful if we can, because it kind of opens this up to everybody,” he said. “You don’t have to care about emissions and the environment to make this choice of a cleaner, quieter plane.”

https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.title: Just Stop Oil: 19 protesters arrested as London marches double in size
https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.text:
Just Stop Oil has doubled the size of its marches in central London as the environmental activists continue their slow-walking campaign on key roads.
Nineteen campaigners were arrested during a series of demonstrations, which began at 8am on Monday with 180 activists in 14 groups marching across the capital, including in Kensington, Islington, Paddington and Whitehall.
Protesters carried placards reading “New oil = murder”, “Hottest June ever” and “Can’t eat oil”. Further marches took place from 10am.
The Metropolitan Police issued dozens of section 12 notices ordering activists to move off the roads and arrested 19 protesters for breaching the notices.
The number of marchers each day in recent weeks has varied between 20 and 70. Those disrupting shops, including the luxury department store Harrods, have numbered between one and two dozen.
Just Stop Oil said on Monday that nearly 200 marchers had taken part, which showed an “escalation of resistance”.
It said officers were following groups before the marches and notices were issued minutes into the protests.
Frances Davis, 20, from Norwich, who was handcuffed by police, said: “I’ve been marching for just under 15 minutes and I’m under arrest for demanding the same thing as the IPCC [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change], the United Nations and the government’s own scientific advisers — and we’ve been ignored. We’ve tried everything else and now I’m in handcuffs just for going on a march.”
On Friday a handful of activists ran on stage with a banner during the opening night of the BBC Proms. Elsewhere three activists threw confetti and jigsaw pieces on stage during the filming of The Last Leg for Channel 4. Earlier in the week marchers also targeted the John Lewis, Selfridges and Hamleys stores in London.
Since February last year more than 2,200 Just Stop Oil campaigners have been arrested.
Just Stop Oil is demanding that the government halt all new licences for oil, gas and coal extraction in the UK. Its activists are marching every day this week in London.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/meet-th.title: Meet the Patriotic Millionaires who want to pay more tax
https://www.thetimes.com/article/meet-th.subtitle: Civil unrest could be on the way unless the most well-off are made to dig deeper, a group of Britain’s richest people say
https://www.thetimes.com/article/meet-th.text:
They say two things are certain in life — death and taxes. And as contrary as it may appear, a growing number of British millionaires are begging Rishi Sunak for more of the latter.
A non-partisan group, Patriotic Millionaires UK (PMUK), has written to the prime minister asking him for a “serious injection of capital” into Britain, which they say should come from the wealthiest. They warn of civil unrest if the inequalities in society are not addressed.
Patriotic Millionaires started in America in 2010 but has spread to Britain in the past two years. The group accepts anyone in the top 1 per cent — those with net assets of over £4 million — and in Britain it has about 40 members.
The group’s emergence comes as Sunak faces pressure because more people are being dragged into the 40 per cent tax band. Some 5.59 million people are expected to pay the higher rate of income tax this year, up from 3.98 million in 2020-21, according to HM Revenue & Customs.
Guy Singh-Watson, the founder of Riverford Organic Farmers, joined PMUK with his wife, Geetie, an award-winning entrepreneur who opened Britain’s first organic pub. “We’ve had the rich getting richer and the poor getting poorer. I want to enjoy my wealth and not think there are other people in desperate poverty,” he said.
“We’re not looking for a revolution, we’re just looking for some appropriate regulations.”
As more people come around to his way of thinking, PMUK is hoping to gain one more member: last month it wrote to the prime minister, inviting him to join.
Not all members have publicly declared their support, but PMUK’s backers include Graham Hobson, the founder of Photobox; the Perry family, who are behind the ready-meal business Cook; Gary Stevenson, a City trader turned inequality economist; Gemma McGough, a technology entrpreneur; and Dale Vince, the green energy industrialist and Just Stop Oil backer.
Some PMUK members fear that Britain’s social fabric is at risk. Jeannie Latenser, who joined with her husband Tim Stumpff, warned of “the potential for economic and political unrest, civil unrest and political instability”.
Julia Davies, a lawyer turned activist who helped to found the group, said: “Disparity in wealth inequality has got so extreme that people are just angry.”
Phil White, another member, added: “I think it’s corrosive because people feel disenfranchised, they feel that society isn’t including them. It’s not meeting their needs, even their basic needs.”
Ian Gregg, whose father founded the Greggs bakery chain, said those who were struggling would be shocked by the situation. Gregg, 84, said: “They must find it difficult when they read of these vast sums of wealth that are being accumulated into fewer and fewer hands.”
“Everybody talks about levelling up and helping the just about managing, but nobody does any damn thing about it,” Gregg said.
Davies said the group was calling for a “moderate wealth tax” of 1-2 per cent on assets of more than £10 million. It is thought this would only apply to the top 0.04 per cent, about 20,000 people.
“I am someone that’s in a fortunate position to have more money than I need to look after myself and my family,” she said. “I genuinely believe that the right thing to do is to pay tax and to be proud to pay tax. I really love my country. I’m very proud of my country and I think it’s become almost sort of unfashionable to say that, but I am.”
The millionaires also back equalising capital gains with income tax rates, applying national insurance to investment income, closing inheritance tax loopholes, reforming the rules on non-dom status, and introducing a 4 per cent tax on share buybacks. They estimate their plans would raise £52.4 billion a year.
A poll for PMUK found more than three quarters of the British public, including 68 per cent of those with £1 million or more in investable assets, backed the wealth tax they propose.
White, now retired after a career in consulting, said: “I’ve not had a single person tell me this is wrong. I don’t think it’s fair that I should really not have to worry about money at all, I can do pretty much anything I want to do, while people are struggling with the cost of living.”
Gregg noted the “sneaky, creeping up of further taxation of ordinary people”.
He said: “A lot of wealthy people have far more than they need. And I think if you’ve got any sort of social conscience, it just doesn’t seem fair. I’ve given most of my wealth away anyway. But I’d be much happier to be paying a little bit more in tax here and there if it was going to make a difference.”
It has been suggested that those who want to could pay more tax voluntarily, or they could donate — as many do — to worthy causes. Davies said while that was “brilliant and fantastic, it’s not democratic”.
She suggested the kind of tax they were proposing would have no impact on the lives of the super wealthy. “Whereas we have been imposing increases in tax on nurses and teachers, and the people who keep our streets clean and safe which will have impacted on whether or not they can take their kids on holiday this year,” she said.
“Tax has become like a dirty word, something that you’re clever if you minimise it. But it’s not clever at all.”
Nick Marple, 54, another PMUK member, said: “Rich people have no idea how poor people live, and how they can afford to live, on a small amount of money. But equally I think the less well off have no idea how much money the rich have got. It’s a very divided society now.”
Akshay Singal, a senior trader at Citigroup, said that if the richest people spent the same amount of time working as they did minimising their tax it would help Britain’s productivity problem. “I work in the financial services industry, and a lot of time seems to be wasted on tax avoidance,” the 36-year-old said.
“You have a lot of people with a lot of money, who spend hours upon hours trying to figure out what the best way is to keep their money.”
Singal said the time being used to “cheat the country” could be put to better use.
This was echoed by Lily Lewis, part of the Lewis family who founded the fashion brand River Island. The 28-year-old said: “The richest are surrounded by legal infrastructures that often advise us on how to pay as little tax as possible in the name of tax efficiency, without questioning the long-term impact on society.
“In order to increase my own tax bracket to what I thought was fair, I even had to enlist the support of a values-aligned advisory firm, Good Ancestor Movement, to help me understand how to actually put into practice my values around tax.”
Latenser added: “I was saying to my friends the other night we could spend hours and hours on this, or we could just fill out the form and pay the taxes. I’m actually proud to pay the taxes I do. Love or hate the name Patriotic Millionaires, but I do think it is patriotic to pay taxes to invest in the kind of country you want.”

https://www.thetimes.com/article/youtube.title: YouTube pranksters turn the tables on Just Stop Oil
https://www.thetimes.com/article/youtube.subtitle: Josh and Archie disrupted a banquet laid on for the eco-activists
https://www.thetimes.com/article/youtube.text:
They are the unlikely pair who led the fightback against the eco-activists Just Stop Oil. Dressed in orange, two pranksters with more than 1.44 million viewers on YouTube stepped in and gave the climate change protesters a dose of their own medicine: disruption.
The two young men who masterminded the Just Stop Pissing Everyone Off countercampaign have revealed they even have the support of members of Extinction Rebellion.
The stunt duo known online as Josh and Archie — Josh Pieters, 29, and Archie Manners, 30 — infiltrated Just Stop Oil with a “mole” and then staged a counterprotest, preventing the activists from blocking traffic in Elephant and Castle, south London.
In printed T-shirts, sporting a play on Just Stop Oil’s branding, Pieters and Manners were joined by a dozen others who surrounded the protesters with a human chain.
They later disrupted another event, a banquet that the protest group had put on, by using rape alarms tied to helium balloons. The stunt was posted on YouTube yesterday.
“We have heard from people who are involved with Extinction Rebellion and other similar groups that they really can’t stand Just Stop Oil, because they are giving whole movements a bad name,” Pieters said. “If you care for climate change, you’ve almost been given a bad name because of Just Stop Oil.”
Manners added: “We’re not alone in thinking — there are a lot of people in the environmental movement thinking, they’re not succeeding, their tactics aren’t working. Thus, something else needs to emerge to ensure that we bring the public with us to tackle climate change.”
Just Stop Oil’s “Beyond F***ed” banquet was held in London on Sunday for activists to “step back, grieve for what will die and disappear but also to celebrate what we have achieved”.
The event was disrupted when the counterprotesters released their balloons, which floated out of reach with blaring alarms attached. People in high-vis jackets had to climb ladders to bring down the balloons.
The public have been broadly supportive of their stunt according to Pieters and Manners, who have identified themselves as the pranksters. According to online profiles, Manners is a great-grandson of Francis Henry Manners, 4th Baron Manners, and studied political sciences at Bristol University. Pieters is from South Africa.
“The reaction has been mostly positive. There’s been some very loud negativity, but the majority of the comments and the reflection of the likes on the YouTube video is massively positive,” Pieters said.
Just Stop Oil also seemed to take the disruption in their stride. “To give credit to them, they took it fairly well,” Pieters said. “I think they understood that what we were doing was exactly what they were doing to other people, so for them to not take it well would be hypocritical.”
Pieters and Manners were keen to state their belief that climate change was the biggest challenge facing their generation, but thought that Just Stop Oil was turning the public away from the cause.
“[Climate change is] a huge, major, major problem, probably the biggest problem facing our generation,” Manners said. “We both care about the environment. We care enough that we realise it’s serious and something needs to be done. They’re achieving nothing. In fact, they’re putting people off.”
https://twitter.com/JustStop_Oil/status/1683437465200148480 They had been planning to target Just Stop Oil for a while, but it was the activists’ stunt at the World Snooker Championship in Sheffield that was the last straw. “The moment that really got us was the snooker, the well-known, environmentally damaging sport of snooker,” Manners said sarcastically. “People saved up a lot of money during a cost of living crisis to go and have a fun afternoon in Sheffield and they ruined one of the tables, massively reducing the enjoyment of all the people there.”
Just Stop Oil praised their “impeccable action design” in a tweet and added: “The alarms they let off . . . were the perfect metaphor for the urgency of the climate crisis.”
The group said in a statement: “We very much enjoyed Josh and Archie’s prank yesterday. Such a good action design — non-violent and ever so slightly disruptive. Their faith in democracy is touching, but the climate crisis needs urgent action today and we simply don’t have time to wait for a new government.”
Extinction Rebellion was invited to comment.
A 13-week long campaign of protest by Just Stop Oil has cost the Metropolitan Police more than £7.7 million, the equivalent of the annual salary of almost 200 police officers (Fiona Hamilton, Crime Editor, writes.)
The Met revealed that a total of 23,597 officer shifts since the end of April had been dedicated to policing the environmental group’s disruption activities and slow marches.
More than 270 people have been arrested during the summer of protests in which JSO protesters blocked roads and interrupted a series of events including the Lord’s Ashes Test, Wimbledon and the Proms. The Met spent a further £7.5 million policing JSO protests between October and December last year.
Assistant commissioner Matt Twist told LBC yesterday: “The Met is a resilient organisation, we’re a large organisation and we’re used to policing protests, but this is quite a chronic thing. In terms of every single day, we’ve got over 150 officers who ordinarily would be policing in local communities, who are policing in and around other parts of London.
“And one of the challenges we have with Just Stop Oil is they don’t tell us where they’re going to protest, they don’t tell us when they’re going to take this action, they don’t engage, which means that we have to put more officers on it than we otherwise would do.”
JSO has said that it will protest until the government stops granting new licences for gas, coal and oil.
Ministers introduced legislation to curtail the activities of environmental protesters including introducing new offences for “locking-on” (people securing themselves to objects). There are also new Public Order Act restrictions aimed at slow walking and giving police greater powers to disperse crowds.
In recent weeks JSO activists have disrupted events including The Open, Wimbledon, the Ashes, the Gallagher Premiership rugby final at Twickenham and the World Snooker Championship. They also took action at Chelsea Flower Show and the London Pride march, disrupted filming of the Channel 4 show The Last Leg, and sprayed orange paint on the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero building in central London.
Twist said that 174 of the 271 people arrested had been charged. It meant that there was a public order and crime team working on putting together cases against them. He added: “So we now have to work towards prosecutions and charges and some cases won’t be heard until 2025.
“It is a significant amount of effort. Again, these are police who could have been doing other things.”
While JSO has accused the Met of turning legitimate protest into crime, Twist insisted that the “right to protest is part of any democratic society and critically important”.
However, he added: “But this isn’t protest, it’s crime. There is a difference. The right to protest is strongly protected, but when you get into deliberately causing serious disruption, that tips over into crime.”
He said that the Met recognised it had to attend protests quickly because “we don’t want people taking the law into their own hands”, but that took up more resources.

https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.title: Oilfield services firm Wood Group lands contract extension in Brunei
https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.text:
Wood Group, the oilfield services and engineering consultancy, has secured a $250 million contract extension from Shell and the government of Brunei.
The Aberdeen-based group said the two-year deal would focus on “the continued rejuvenation” of the top 20 offshore energy assets owned by Brunei Shell Petroleum to maximise production and efficiency.
Brunei Shell Petroleum (BSP) is a 50-50 joint venture between Shell, the FTSE 100 oil major, and the government of Brunei. The company is the largest oil and gas producer in Brunei.
Wood, officially John Wood Group, is a FTSE 250 company which reported profits of $385 million last year and employs more than 35,000 people worldwide.
Wood said the contract extension to February 2026 included “brownfield engineering, procurement, construction and commissioning services as well as the management of its offshore marine fleet”.
About 1,500 people are employed under the contract, about two thirds of whom are in Brunei.
Ken Gilmartin, chief executive of Wood, said: “Wood is pleased to continue supporting BSP’s offshore assets in the next phase of its rejuvenation project to upgrade core assets, which account for around 80 per cent of BSP’s production, making this work critically important to the company.”
Brunei Shell Petroleum accounts for about 90 per cent of the country’s revenues from the oil and gas industry, which in turn accounts for about half of the country’s economy.
Shares in Wood Group rose by 3 per cent or 4p to 139¼p. Earlier this year Wood’s shares hit highs of more than 220p as it was the target of a series of takeover approaches from Apollo Global, the US private equity firm. After rejecting four offers it engaged with Apollo on a 240p-per-share approach only for Apollo to decide against making a firm offer for the group, leading to Wood’s share price falling back.
Separately yesterday, Wood Group’s offices in Surrey and Aberdeen were targeted by protesters from Extinction Rebellion, the climate change activist group. Two activists were arrested for alleged criminal damage at the Surrey site after spraying fake black oil over the office entrance.
The campaigners want Wood to cut ties with the oil and gas industry and accuse the company of misusing a £430 million taxpayer-backed green transition loan after reports by The Guardian and Point Source last month that the group had expanded its fossil fuel business and shrunk its renewables business since receiving the loan.
Wood said it remained committed to its role in the energy transition, but that this included helping oil and gas clients to decarbonise their operations. It has also cut its own operational emissions.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: George Osborne’s wedding brings dad dancing and confetti protest
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.subtitle: The former chancellor’s wedding party was a throwback to coalition days
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
As George Osborne celebrated his second marriage, dancing with some old friends and foes to Things Can Only Get Better by D:Ream, the unofficial theme for New Labour, a guest remarked: “It was more like a marriage of all the centrist dads.”
The guest added: “It was like a throwback to the coalition years, but this time they were all dancing together rather than squabbling.”
Dancing with the former chancellor on Saturday was Ed Balls, his Labour foe who has become a friend, and Sir Danny Alexander, the Lib Dem who was chief secretary to the Treasury during the coalition, as well as Michael Gove, Matt Hancock and Sajid Javid, his former Tory cabinet colleagues.
Also on the dance floor was Yvette Cooper, Balls’s wife and the shadow home secretary. “It was like a scene out of Spitting Image,” another guest said. “But everyone was having a great time.”
The day was full of political nods to those at the wedding of Osborne, 52, and Thea Rogers, 40, who served as chief of staff in the Treasury and was credited with overhauling his image.
As the couple completed their vows at the 14th-century St Mary’s Church in Bruton, Somerset, Beethoven’s Ode to Joy — the European Union anthem — was played out, triggering a chorus of chuckles and awkward glances towards Gove, one of few Brexiteers at the event.
“It was all a bit of a throwback to the coalition years and the Remain campaign,” a guest said. Osborne’s political ruthlessness was also alluded to in more than one of the speeches.
Lord Finkelstein, the Times columnist and Osborne’s best man, joked during his speech that he had watched as he hovered over the wedding cake with a knife earlier in the evening. “It’s the first time I’ve seen George unsure of where to put the knife in,” he said.
Lord Hague of Richmond, the former foreign secretary and also a Times columnist, was among several guests invited to make short speeches at a dinner on Friday night. He nicknamed the groom “George GPT” because he was like a political robot with never-ending ideas and the knack of always correctly predicting which way the parliamentary votes would go.
Matthew Gould, Osborne’s friend who is the head of London Zoo and Britain’s former ambassador to Israel, spoke at the dinner that was held at the five-star Newt hotel and spa in Castle Cary, as did Rogers’s friend Kate Garvey, a former aide to Sir Tony Blair. Guests reunited on Sunday morning around the spa’s pool.
Other guests included Nick Robinson, the Radio 4 presenter and Rogers’s former boss when she was a producer at the BBC before being recruited by Osborne. Jon Sopel and Emily Maitlis, who were friends with Rogers at the BBC, were also in attendance.
One of Osborne’s close friends, Pete Davies, who was best man at his wedding to his first wife Frances, arrived by helicopter. Mark Carney, the former governor of the Bank of England, was also one of the guests.
The wedding reception was held at Hauser & Wirth, the art gallery exhibition venue in Bruton, close to where the couple recently bought a five-bedroom, grade II listed home. Guests were treated to a lavish barbecue in the manicured gardens of the hotel.
Osborne’s four children all attended the wedding, including the two from his first marriage, Luke, 22, and Liberty, 20.
Osborne and Rogers’s two children — Arthur, who is seven months old, and Beau, who turns two next week — were there, along with the family’s dog Albi, a fox-red labrador.
“It was a joyous vibe, with the kids and even his dog at the church,” a guest said.
David Cameron, the former prime minister who attended with his wife Samantha, filmed the couple on his mobile as they walked under a tunnel of well-wishers throwing confetti. He failed, however, to catch a protester who threw her own orange confetti on the newlyweds, as the campaign group Just Stop Oil has done at recent sporting events.
The activist ambushed the couple as they left the church so the guests were oblivious to the slight hiccup to proceedings.
While Just Stop Oil “applauded and thanked” the woman, the group said she was not one of their members. One of the group’s insiders expressed relief that the “lone-wolf” activist was not one of their number.
The action provoked a wave of outrage from across the political spectrum. Rachel Reeves, Labour’s shadow chancellor, said it was “pathetic”. She added: “They are not building support for their cause. They are doing the exact opposite. It is counterproductive.” Separately, a bigger shadow hanging over the wedding was the vicious anonymous email sent to guests last week that made a number of unsubstantiated claims about the couple’s private lives.
Osborne has asked the police to investigate, describing the missive as “part of a very serious campaign of ongoing harassment”. The couple are said to know the identity of the person behind the email.
On Saturday night, however, the newlyweds and their varied guests put any past differences behind them. As Osborne once said, they were “all in this together” while the centrist dads danced the night away.

image.caption: George Osborne, the former chancellor, married Thea Rogers on Saturday in a lavish ceremonyFINNBARR WEBSTER/GETTY IMAGES

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Swampy at 50: Just Stop Oil tactics just aren’t cricket
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
When the England wicketkeeper Jonny Bairstow was carrying a Just Stop Oil protester off the pitch at Lord’s on Wednesday morning, Daniel Hooper was strimming verges in south Wales.
The eco-warrior otherwise known as Swampy, whose subterranean sit-ins made him a household name in the late 1990s, was doing community service for his part in tunnelling under an HS2 construction site in Wendover, Buckinghamshire, in 2021.
As he whacked weeds, word spread among the group of criminals that a celebrity was among them. Was it really him, one man asked Hooper, who is 50.
“I just said, ‘Yeah, it’s me’,” Hooper tells me as we sit in a café in Carmarthen, in a brief window between strimming and an appointment with his probation officer. “And the man just said, ‘Fair play’. I think most people are supportive nowadays.”
Yet Hooper, who wears a chunky red hoodie and a home-cut fringe (the dreadlocks are long gone) has thought a lot lately about support for environmental activism, and the kinds of tactics that work — or don’t.
Two weeks ago he joined a new group that rejects the tactics of Just Stop Oil. The Climate Majority Project (CMP) says it wants to promote action in politics, business and society by representing those who feel alienated by road blocking and the spreading of orange powder over hallowed sporting grounds.
Hooper, who lives off-grid at a nearby commune, won’t bash Just Stop Oil, but nor does he support them. “I couldn’t speak for or against what they do, but I definitely think the time has come to bring communities together,” he says.
The tacit repudiation — by Swampy of all people — comes at an interesting time for the wider movement. Last weekend, Trevor Neilson, a wealthy Californian entrepreneur and big Just Stop Oil funder, told The Sunday Times of his growing unease about their guerilla tactics. “I absolutely believe that it has now become counterproductive,” he said.
Would Swampy sit in a road or run on to the pitch at Lord’s? “The people doing it are obviously brave and passionate, but I wouldn’t have thought so, no.”
Yet Hooper also agrees with the damning assessment of Lord Deben, the Tory peer formerly known as John Gummer. On Wednesday, Deben, the outgoing chairman of the Climate Change Committee, criticised the UK’s “utterly unacceptable” lack of progress on climate action. Two days later, Lord Goldsmith of Richmond Park resigned as an environment minister, accusing Rishi Sunak of being “uninterested” in climate change.
Hooper is equally frustrated but thinks that Just Stop Oil has reached the limit of its potential to grab attention. Now, he says, “We need a broad range of people to get together and say, ‘How are we going to do this?’ Hopefully [CMP] will at least assist in doing that, and bring people in from different walks of life, including myself and, dare I say it, a Tory peer.”
He’s now referring to Lord Randall of Uxbridge, Theresa May’s former environment adviser, who is among an eclectic range of CMP backers. They also include the TV presenter Chris Packham, the author Michael Rosen and Lewis Pugh, the endurance swimmer.
A staff of a dozen, led by its co-director, Rupert Read, a philosophy professor and former Extinction Rebellion spokesman, is inviting new funding to, among other things, support community projects, an “MP watch” programme to hold politicians to account and partnerships with the advertising industry to promote shifts in consumer behaviour.
Hooper’s involvement so far has been to lend the group his name. He has not yet met Randall, who last week acknowledged his unlikely new bedfellow: “While I would be happy to have a chat with Swampy about his views, it doesn’t necessarily mean I’m going to jump into a hole with him.”
Would the new, moderate Swampy have a chat with Randall? “I’ll save a lock-on tube for him!” he says with an impish grin that has not faded in 25 years. “That was a joke, but, look, there’s got to be common ground. The message is out there, now we need to get the job done.”
It all feels like a long way from Newbury, where, in 1996, a 23-year-old Hooper, the son of Daily Mail-reading parents from Buckinghamshire, got a taste for activism at a protest against a new bypass.
In 1997, Hooper emerged from a tunnel under a dual carriageway scheme in Devon and achieved instant notoriety (he would also earn a slap on the wrist from the local magistrate Mary Cameron, David’s mother). He chuckled his way through Have I Got News For You and watched as Coronation Street introduced an eco-warrior in his honour called Spider.
He even became a pinup as an antidote to 1990s lad culture. The editor of Cosmopolitan called him “sexy”. Hooper says: “I was getting called a style guru while wearing old clothes I’d probably got out of a skip.”
Fame grated and Hooper retreated from the media glare, settling at Tipi Valley, a commune where he built a house, started a small forestry enterprise, and had a family with his wife Clare (his three children are aged 12 to 18).
He says his comeback wasn’t planned, but it felt necessary. In 2020, he joined HS2 protesters — including his then 16-year-old son Rory — in tunnels at Euston station in London and then at Wendover. “Hopefully that has made an impact, because I think nearly everyone is against HS2,” he says.
Hooper, who tends to vote for Plaid Cymru, isn’t sure how far popular support for meaningful climate action has shifted since the 1990s. He’s appalled by recent legislation to limit peaceful protest. “It’s through direct action that the most meaningful change has happened,” he says. “Making laws to stop it is ludicrous. If I were in a tunnel now I’d get up to three years in prison.” Would he take that risk?
“I wouldn’t say I’d never do it again but you’ve got to think about how much gets stopped compared to how much you could put up with . . . Spending two years in jail while my kids are the age that they are probably isn’t a good idea.”
When he isn’t working, campaigning or tending his vegetable patch, Hooper enjoys a drink in the local community pub. He’s part of a fell-running club. He’s charming and cheerful, and, while he has clearly evolved, his fighting spirit still surfaces.
Right now, he’s unsure what his weekly probation meetings might achieve. “Are they gonna try and rehabilitate me?” he asks before running to his appointment. “Am I supposed to say I’m sorry for what I’ve done and I realise the errors of my ways? Because I don’t. We were doing a good thing.”

https://www.thetimes.com/article/keir-st.title: Keir Starmer promises compulsory arts or sport until 16
https://www.thetimes.com/article/keir-st.subtitle: Labour leader calls for a more creative curriculum in speech marred by climate hecklers
https://www.thetimes.com/article/keir-st.text:
All children will have to study creative arts or sport until they are 16 under a Labour government because AI makes learning code pointless, Sir Keir Starmer has said.
In a flagship speech on education which was briefly derailed by climate protesters, Starmer announced plans to shake up the national curriculum to focus more on creative subjects to teach the skills needed to capitalise on modern technology.
Confidence, communication, teamwork and problem-solving are more important for children than “out-of-date” IT lessons, Starmer said as he set out plans to put speaking clearly and fluently at the heart of the curriculum.
In a deliberate provocation to the Labour left, Starmer quoted Michael Gove, the Conservative former education secretary, to criticise “the soft bigotry of low expectations” for poorer children.
“I don’t agree with everything he did in education, clearly, but when he said that — it was an important strike against the class ceiling, an acknowledgement that school standards are the most fundamental front line in the battle for more opportunity,” Starmer said.• Starmer wants speaking lessons for all pupils
In a personal section, Starmer drew on his own background to say his desire to improve education was “our core purpose and my personal cause”. Citing his parents’ pebble-dashed semi, “with Mum, Dad, four kids, four dogs and a blue Ford Cortina outside” he said that he was able to rise from a working-class background to lead the Crown Prosecution Service.
Jibing at the Tories that “there is more than a touch of the 1970s about our economic situation right now”, Starmer suggested that journeys such as his were harder today.
As well as criticising contemporary economic insecurity, he also condemned a “pernicious” assumption that working-class children should lower their ambitions. He said this “class ceiling” was “about a fundamental lack of respect, a snobbery that too often extends into adulthood,” citing his own father, a toolmaker. “Whenever anyone asked that old question ‘what do you do for a living’ — I could see him visibly pull away. He felt looked down upon, disrespected. It chipped away at his esteem.”
While praising New Labour for having “the best record on education in the history of our country,” he acknowledged that the Blair government “didn’t eradicate the snobbery that looks down on vocational education, didn’t drain the well of disrespect that this creates, and that cost us”.
Starmer argued that lack of confidence held back poorer children, saying “the inability to speak fluently is one of the biggest barriers to opportunity,” as he said that oracy would become as central to the curriculum as literacy. “Confident speaking gives you a steely core, and an inner belief to make your case in any environment,” he said.
Starmer also argued that developing digital skills required them to become part of teaching in all subjects rather than hived off to separate lessons, as he stressed that creative skills were vital to make the most of new technology.
“The old way — learning out-of-date IT, on 20-year-old computers — doesn’t work, but neither does the new fashion, that every kid should be a coder, when artificial intelligence will blow that future away,” he said.
“All around the world, the best in class are rethinking their curricula, and every one of them is putting greater creativity front and centre, including countries like Estonia and Singapore.” He promised to “get children studying a creative arts subject, or sport, until they are 16”. Labour said the creative subjects would include music, art and drama.
Starmer’s speech threatened to be derailed soon after it began when two of the young people standing behind him revealed themselves to be climate activists. Unfurling a banner declaring “Green New Deal now,” they accused him of backtracking on plans to spend £28 billion a year on green measures. “Young people want action,” one protester told Starmer. “We need a green new deal right now.”
Starmer replied: “Will you just let me finish this and then come and talk to you about it?” As they were escorted off stage by venue staff, Starmer then told the audience: “I think they may have missed the fact that the last mission I launched was on clean power by 2030 which is the single most effective way to get the green future that they and many others want.”
Green New Deal Rising, a movement of 16 to 35-year-olds calling for a ten-year climate plan including a “permanent and progressive windfall tax for polluters,” claimed responsibility for the demonstration.
Dieudonné Bila, a student who was one of the protesters, said: “I disrupted Keir Starmer’s speech because I desperately want to see a future government committed to protecting people here and all over the world from the climate crisis . . . if Keir Starmer wants the support of young people like us he needs to set out a bold vision for the future that gets to the root causes of the problems we are facing.”
The group said they had invited Starmer and Rachel Reeves, the shadow chancellor, to meet them to discuss their demands for the party’s manifesto but the Labour Party had not replied.
Earlier, Starmer had significantly hardened his criticism of Just Stop Oil’s campaign tactics, which he said “is totally counterproductive”. He told Times Radio: “I can’t wait for them to stop their antics, frankly. They’re interrupting iconic sporting events that are part of our history, tradition and massively looked forward to across the nation. I absolutely condemn the way they go about their tactics. And I have to say it’s riddled with an arrogance that only they have the sort of right to force their argument on other people in this way.”
After his speech was disrupted by climate activists, Starmer told the audience: “I just think they need to just stop. Particularly this last week, they’ve been interrupting iconic sporting events, causing massive disruption. There’s a huge arrogance involved, that they’re the only people that understand the argument, that their tactics are going to win.”

https://www.thetimes.com/article/are-we-.title: Are we to blame for the heatwaves? Friederike Otto can tell us
https://www.thetimes.com/article/are-we-.text:
It is remarkable how Dr Friederike Otto manages to keep her cool while ecosystems around the world are literally losing theirs. The physicist is at the vanguard of an emerging discipline of climate science that takes any extreme weather event and seeks to work out, rapidly, the extent to which man-made climate change is the culprit.
Every time there is a killer heatwave or freak flood she appears on the airwaves, patiently explaining whether each one was made more likely or more intense by human-induced climate change. Yet despite all the breakthroughs in her field, despite all the government pledges to halt global warming, here we still are, hurtling towards dangerous increases in global temperatures. She must feel like the Cassandra of climate change. Does it sometimes feel like hollering into an abyss?
She smiles politely. “I do sometimes feel quite angry. I can rationalise why we don’t see political change because you can make a lot of money by selling and digging up oil and gas. We have been brainwashed to think that the definition of freedom is to live in concrete and drive a car. That is a very stupid definition of freedom.”
So Otto has made it her duty to communicate the causes of these events, answering the question that comes whenever Athens is ablaze or the heat strikes down people in the street in Italy, as has happened this week: is climate change to blame?
The other question she gets is where she draws the line between being a scientist and an activist. “If you have the knowledge and if you can explain why we see these heatwaves now, and don’t do it, that would be quite negligent. So if that makes me an activist, then yes, I guess I am. What will be the alternative? Be a ‘passive-ist’ and just keep quiet?
“I’m not a member of any [political] party. I’m not chaining myself to the motorway, although,” she says, raising an eyebrow, “it is sometimes tempting. My role as a scientist is a different one but I don’t think you can work on climate change and think ‘Oh, yeah, what the government is currently doing is splendid’.”
She believes that Just Stop Oil protesters, far from being troublemakers, are the sane ones in a mad world. “What they want is really not radical. But that so many people think it is — that is shocking. They just want to keep within the targets which this country, as well as most other countries in the world, agreed to in the Paris Agreement. So it’s not something outrageous.”
She also believes that Greta Thunberg has done us all a favour. “We’re still not acting in the way that we need to but we are talking about it. It’s just not something you can ignore any more. That’s a huge achievement and that’s because of her.”
Otto, 40, is cool and composed. She dresses casually — green Converse trainers and a tangle of colourful bracelets on her wrist, made by her teenage son — but her automatic reply set up on her email, warning that “emails addressed to Mrs Otto will be forwarded to my mum” suggest the steeliness of an academic who was named by Time as one of the 100 most influential people in the world.
She grew up in “an old cottage in the middle of nowhere”, near the Baltic port of Kiel, the daughter of a teacher and a biologist, before doing a PhD in Berlin and ten years working on environmental change at the University of Oxford. Her career trajectory mirrors how the climate emergency has shifted in the public consciousness. The mantra used to be that no single “natural” weather event could be directly linked to carbon emissions. Thanks to the World Weather Attribution (WWA) project, which she and her late colleague Geert Jan van Oldenborgh founded in 2015, scientists can now speak confidently about the degree to which climate change plays a role in individual emergencies.
It began with an idea, mooted by a fellow climate scientist who watched his home flood in 2004. Who or what was liable for this local event, he wondered. “In the same way that you can say smoking increases the likelihood of cancer, you should be able to say this flood was more likely and/or more intense because of climate change,” Otto explains. They developed “extreme event attribution”, which uses computer modelling and real observations of weather events to compare the world with and without the roughly 1C rise in temperatures caused by humanity so far.
“We are the only group in the world doing this regularly on a rapid basis.” Crucially, they don’t wait for peer review, the idea being that their reports will have a greater chance of strong-arming policymakers into action if published while the havoc is still raw. This has become less controversial as the modelling has become more sophisticated. The work “is now mostly seen as an important part of climate science”, Otto says from her office at the Grantham Institute, Climate Change and the Environment, at Imperial College, London. It is now clear that man-made factors have made every heatwave today more intense and more likely. The temperatures across the western Mediterranean last week would have been “almost impossible” before humans began burning fossil fuels.
Her team at WWA has found that human factors made the UK’s first 40C day (last July) “at least ten times more likely”; the severe Horn of Africa drought and the exceptional April Mediterranean heatwave this year “at least 100 times more likely”; and the rising temperatures across Siberia “at least 600 times more likely”.
Their research is also being used in legal cases. Their study that Australian bushfires were made 30 per cent more likely by climate change helped survivors to win their legal battle against the state environmental regulator last year. It was the first time a court had found an Australian government agency to be failing in its duty to address global warming. “That’s a start,” she says.
A county in Oregon is suing fossil fuel companies, including Exxon Mobil, Shell, BP and their business partners, in an attempt to hold them responsible for the heatwave that killed 69 people in the northwest US in 2021. In the prosecutors’ arsenal will be WWA’s research that this “heat dome” would have been virtually impossible without global warming.
She doesn’t expect any single legal case to be a game-changer “but what they show is that the impacts of climate change are here and now and you can measure them”. It is equally important to record when climate change is not a driving factor, she adds, as was the case with the recent flooding of the northern Italian region of Emilia Romagna, and the 2021 drought in Madagascar. “It’s really important to highlight that climate change is a huge problem but not everything that’s happening is because of climate change.”
She says the fingerprints of climate change are easier to find in food prices, for example, than migration. It is “straightforward” to show how the heatwave in Pakistan and India last year destroyed crops, led to an export ban and drove up the food prices in our shopping trolleys, she says. Migration is different. “For people to actually leave their country they need economic means.” While climate change might drive internal displacement, “more extreme weather means that people have less money and are less able to go [abroad]. So it traps people more than it really fuels migration outside of borders”.
The Paris Agreement in 2015 was the first legally binding global pact to tackle global warming. This week one of the most eminent environmental scientists, Professor Sir Robert Watson, shared his stark belief that its key target to keep temperature increases below 1.5C was beyond reach. “In fact,” he said, “I’m very pessimistic about achieving even 2C.
Otto has a different take. “I think fixating on 1.5C is not helpful. 1.2C is already dangerous for many and deadly for some. In order to reach 1.5C or 2C or any other temperature goal we need to get to net zero, so that is what we need to focus on, cutting emissions as fast as possible. 1.5C would be great and, from a physics point of view, possible but current policies bring us to about 3C. But if we try for 1.5C and achieve 1.6C or 1.7C that will still be very much better than now getting stuck in a rhetoric that it’s too late and continue to do more or less nothing.”
The frustration of these scientists reminds me of Don’t Look Up, the satirical 2021 disaster film starring Jennifer Lawrence and Leonardo DiCaprio as astronomers driven insane by the world’s refusal to heed their warnings about an asteroid.
“I hate that film,” Otto sighs. “Because climate change is not an asteroid. It is lots and lots of small death, happening now. It’s not a massive cliff we fall off in the future that we can solve with one big tech fix. It’s a problem that we can only solve politically and socially. Too many people are waiting for the asteroid to fall on our head.”
Let’s imagine her becoming world leader tomorrow. What would she do first?
“Stop burning fossil fuels. A massive investment in insulating homes because that will mean the demand for energy will go down [so] not so many people will die in heatwaves. And decarbonising traffic because we know exactly how to do it. We know how to build trains that run on electricity rather than diesel. They are the really low-hanging fruits that will improve health and quality of living for lots of people and at the same time, get emissions down.”
There is one reason to be cheerful: “It’s not as if we can’t do anything about it. We have all the knowledge and all the technology that we need.”
Born August 29, 1982
Education Physics at University of Potsdam, PhD in philosophy of science from Free University of Berlin
Career She joined the University of Oxford in 2011 as director of the Environmental Change Institute. She co-founded World Weather Attribution in 2014 and in 2019 wrote Angry Weather, a bestselling book. She was one of the scientists who wrote the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s sixth assessment report. Also works with lawyers to hold polluting companies and governments accountable. In 2021 she was included in Time’s annual list of the 100 most influential people and joined Imperial College London as a senior lecturer.
Family Lives in London with her son.
Twitter or Threads? Twitter, I can’t face starting again
Baltic Sea or the Bahamas? Baltic
Barbie or Oppenheimer? Barbie
London or Berlin? London!
Uber or Lime bike? Never a car
Pint or pinot noir? A pint of pinot
Converse or DMs? Both

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/film/ar.title: Am I the only film critic who hasn’t fallen for Tom Cruise’s puppy dog eyes?
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/film/ar.text:
I am the only “Top Critic” on Rotten Tomatoes to have given the new Mission: Impossible movie a bad review. This fact does not bother me because, bar a deftly executed train wreck finale, it’s a pretty awful film. That negative review, however, seems to have bothered a lot of other people, who have contacted me via Twitter, email and Times online to let me know that I am a “clickbait” contrarian, a “hater” of mainstream entertainment, someone who should be sacked and, crucially, a spiteful person to have denied Tom Cruise’s Mission: Impossible, Dead Reckoning Part One a perfect 100 per cent “certified fresh” score on the review aggregation website.
Indeed, an amused friend sent me a screen grab of the Rotten Tomatoes Dead Reckoning review page, which features 41 bright red “fresh” icons, complete with blurby praise, surrounding my one, lonely green splodge of “rotten” misery.
Now, I was never great at analytics at university, but I’m almost sure that, statistically speaking, this should not happen. The only thing that would account for a data spread this anomalous would be if I was basically deranged and Dead Reckoning was the kind of ineffable cinematic masterpiece not seen since Citizen Kane — although even then the Top Critics of 1941 were undecided, calling that film devoid of “entertainment value” and with an ending that “fizzled”. No, something else is clearly afoot here, and this is my best guess . . .
Cruise, through sheer force of personality, has convinced the world that he is the one true saviour of cinema. He has spent the past two years, since the worst times of Covid, pinging around the planet, first with Top Gun: Maverick (a film that I loved, by the way), now Dead Reckoning, banging the drum for the big-screen experience and for his vital role in keeping it alive. He has made endless personal appearances in the UK, including showy stops at everything from a Rolling Stones concert in Hyde Park to the Goodwood Festival of Speed and, via headline-grabbing helicopter ride, the Wimbledon men’s final. And all the time, whenever there’s a media crew within grab range, he says, earnestly, with puppy dog eyes on full beam, like he did on Graham Norton: “I am always thinking about the audience. I want to entertain them and give them a new adventure every time.”
● Stunts, Scientology and blockbusters — who is the real Tom Cruise?
That is, psychologically speaking, quite a lot for an audience, any audience, even an audience of film critics, to carry. That burden. Cruise is always thinking about us. He’s like a vulnerable ex-boyfriend who won’t stop texting us with updates on his boring-ass life. And so it’s only natural to think, “Damn! I hope I like his new movie. I don’t want to hurt his feelings. He seems kind of sensitive. Now, where did I put that five-star review?”
In truth many of those red icons on the Rotten Tomatoes page are actually soft three-star reviews that read, “Film’s not as good as the last one, pretty poor in places but, hey, the Cruiser is back! Doing what the Cruiser does best! Er, do you think he’ll like that?”
It’s probably instructional, at this point, to compare Cruise to his Hollywood peer Brad Pitt. Pitt was in the UK, at Silverstone, over the weekend, filming scenes for his Formula One racing movie Apex. And though that film is being made by two of Tom Cruise’s regular collaborators, the producer Jerry Bruckheimer and the director of Top Gun: Maverick, Joseph Kosinski, there was no Cruise-like antics from Pitt. Instead he laid low, took a few selfies with fans and made no speeches whatsoever about the importance of cinema. He doesn’t do that. Never has. Doesn’t tell the audience that he’s thinking about them either. And the result? His last starring film, Bullet Train, was hammered on Rotten Tomatoes, with nearly half the reviews represented as miserable green splodges. I was one of those splodges. Well, it was a bad movie and I had a job to do. It’s not like I’m a clickbait contrarian.
I see Just Stop Oil and its disciples are finally getting creative. Only days after it crashed Wimbledon, a devious superannuated protester interrupted the nuptials of George Osborne to Thea Rogers in the West Country hamlet of Bruton, Somerset. The twist here is that, instead of splattering the pair in orange paint as they emerged from the church, she merely shuffled up behind them and shook some very on-message orange confetti over their shoulders. Which was almost sweet.
What’s next? Orange holy water at a celebrity baptism? Orange party poppers at an A-list birthday party? Orange champagne? Orange, er, juice? And though I appreciate this softer, kinder approach, I feel that JSO needs to rethink the rhetoric of its protesters, who currently and consistently bleat, “I’m doing this for my grandchildren!” Yep, while your grandchildren are floating down the Thames on a tiny blob of Arctic ice they’ll be thinking, “Thank God Granddad interrupted Daria Saville and Katie Boulter for two minutes on court 18 back in Wimbledon 2023. That made all the difference!”
Pet owners, according to a new study from the Centre for Economics and Business Research, are suckers. Well, not literally. They will just, apparently, agree to pay more money to make sure that their homes are “burglar-proof” than people without pets. Hmm. If only there was a way to make your home burglar-proof and to have a pet without spending extra money? Try my way! Have a 50kg Leonberger as a pet! They sit by the front door, making themselves perfectly visible to all manner of delivery drivers, cold callers, meter testers, energy company representatives and even, yes, potential burglars. And by their sheer size alone (actually a distraction from the underlying nature of a soft and soppy pussycat) they seem to say, “Go on, burgle us, I dare you!”

https://www.thetimes.com/article/i-hate-.title: ‘I hate tree-huggers’ — Keir Starmer explodes over green policy
https://www.thetimes.com/article/i-hate-.subtitle: Labour’s leader and his allies are unhappy their economic focus is being jeopardised by the party’s ‘eco-warriors’
https://www.thetimes.com/article/i-hate-.text:
Ed Miliband gave an animated Powerpoint presentation to the shadow cabinet on his revolutionary energy policies, speaking excitedly of the hope and change he believed they would bring.
His reception from Sir Keir Starmer, however, was decidedly lukewarm.
“[Starmer] thanked him for his presentation, but said he wasn’t interested in hope and change, he was more interested in creating sustainable new jobs to replace jobs in old sectors that were being lost,” said a source. “He then said he was not interested in tree-huggers, before adding to everyone’s surprise, ‘In fact, I hate tree-huggers’.”
The comments surprised some in the meeting, which took place the day after Starmer gave a speech on energy strategy in Aberdeen last month, but they are symptomatic of the divide that exists between him and Miliband.
Those close to the leader believe it is the economic challenge, not climate change, the party needs to focus on. They see Miliband as an eco-warrior who is more interested in the green agenda than the party’s central priorities of jobs, bills and energy security.
A shadow cabinet minister said: “Keir is always trying to anchor the party. Ed will always try to toe the line by saying that the party’s priorities are jobs, bills, energy security and climate change in that order. He can’t help himself, he is a hopey-changey kind of person.”
Morgan McSweeney, Labour’s election chief, is frustrated by those in the party pushing the green policies.A source close to him said: “He sees everything through the prism of electoral success. He sees everything else as a distraction. He wants to throw the excess baggage off the boat and just concentrate on the economy.
“He thinks the focus, for example, on the party’s pledge to end all North Sea gas and oil licences has been an unhelpful distraction, and something the Tories can easily weaponise.
“In contrast, he wants to see more focus on the party’s Bidenomics-led policies, which amounts to an ambitious plan for creating the industries and jobs of the future.”
Rachel Reeves, the shadow chancellor, and Pat McFadden, the shadow chief secretary to the Treasury, are among the “sceptics” who think the focus on a green agenda is complicating Labour’s key messages. A source familiar with their thinking said: “They want to talk about economic change not climate change.”
Another member of the shadow cabinet said the party risked shooting itself in the foot by becoming obsessed with the climate-change agenda, where there are “very few votes”.
The row has been rumbling on since last year’s annual party conference in Liverpool, when Starmer’s most senior advisers, including Deborah Mattinson, his director of strategy, and Peter Hyman, a former aide, wanted to change the colour of the party’s red rose emblem to green. They argued that commitment to the environment and “green stuff” should be one of the Labour leader’s overarching messages.
They were overruled by others, including the unions, who thought the idea was “mad”, given the inflation crisis.
A senior party source said: “Much of the tensions that exist now are a throwback to conference. There have been those who have been pushing the green agenda, but recent events have shown that tactic could easily backfire, and there is an overriding sense among most in the shadow cabinet that we need to strip everything back and talk about our core messages.”
In recent weeks, Labour has faced scrutiny of policies seen to have been the brainchild of Miliband, including the plan for £28 billion a year in capital spending on green growth and a commitment to ban new oil and gas developments in the North Sea.
Starmer is also under pressure from the Conservative Party for taking £1.5 million from Dale Vince, a vegan ex-hippy and green energy industrialist who also donates money to the direct action group Just Stop Oil. The leader’s office insists that Vince, who was ushered in as a donor under Miliband’s leadership, has “absolutely no influence on policy”. In an interview with Times Radio on Thursday, the Labour leader condemned the “arrogance” of the group’s tactics, and said: “I can’t wait for them to stop their antics.”
However, by far the biggest headache comes from Sadiq Khan’s plans to expand the ultra low emission zone (Ulez) for vehicles to outer London.
Last week, Starmer exposed internal divisions when he backed the party’s candidate in the Uxbridge by-election who said the expansion should be delayed.
Danny Beales said it was “not the right time to extend the Ulez scheme to outer London”, in a direct challenge to Khan, the Labour mayor. Starmer was asked if he agreed with Beales, and he said the party’s candidate was “right” to “stick up” for his would-be constituents.
The split within Labour mirrors one in the Conservative Party. Lord Goldsmith resigned as a minister last month, accusing Rishi Sunak of being “uninterested” in the environment. He told Channel 4 in an interview last week: “[Sunak’s] not in the net-zero sceptic camp . . . he’s just not motivated by these issues, he’s not interested, they don’t move him.”
Lord Frost, the former Brexit secretary, is among the most vocal sceptics. He used a speech in May to argue that Britain’s path to delivering net zero is “inevitably wasteful and damaging”.
Starmer is now waking up to the disconnect between his own party’s political and economic objectives.
It is understood that he will visit Aberdeen this summer to talk to industry and union figures, after criticism of the party’s proposals to freeze North Sea oil and gas licences. Critics believe Labour has fallen into the same trap as the SNP — which has embraced the green agenda and has Green Party MSPs in the Holyrood cabinet — and risks losing votes.
A senior Labour figure said: “It will just take one North Sea oil worker to stand up and say that despite being a lifetime Labour voter, they are going to vote Tory because of this policy and it could be game over. We need to be the party that can sow the green shoots of recovery rather than the party of tree-huggers.”
Rachel Reeves, the shadow chancellor further watered down Labour’s plans to invest in green technologies of the future.
The party had promised to spend £28 billion a year on green investment from the first year of entering power, but last month scaled back its plans, saying it would only meet the commitment by the middle of its first parliament in power.
Reeves failed to guarantee that the party would meet its £28 billion green spending pledge even by the end of the first parliament, insisting it was dependent on whether it had balanced the books.
The shadow chancellor’s refusal to commit to the policy, which was the centrepiece of her first speech to Labour’s party conference as shadow chancellor in September 2021, is a further sign of the party’s determination to prove its fiscal credibility.
Asked whether Labour is committed to spending £28 billion on green investment by the end of its first parliament in power, Reeves told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: “We’re confident that we can get there.”
Pressed again on whether she can guarantee the spending commitment, she said: “We’re committed to it but it’s subject to our fiscal rules.”
Reeves, who would become the first female chancellor in history if Labour wins the next election, added: “I’ve always been clear that all our policies, including investing in the industries of the future and boosting our energy security, are subject to our fiscal rules, which means paying for day to day spending through tax receipts and getting debt down as a share of the economy.”
